formal_statement.reads: For every input: when the declared precondition holds, the computation returns Ok carrying some value; when it does not hold, the computation returns a typed Refusal carrying a reason and the evidence behind it. Both branches are total; there is no third, silent outcome.

relationship_triad.requires: A declared precondition for the Ok path and a typed Refusal carrying a reason and evidence on every other path, including missing dependencies and undefined values.
relationship_triad.refuses: An inadmissible number or silent NaN returned where no precondition was checked.

doctrine_entities.title: Provenance propagation and non-interference
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Data labels propagate along flows; untrusted labels reach privileged sinks only through declared transforms satisfying sink policy.
doctrine_entities.statement: Data labels propagate along flows; untrusted labels reach privileged sinks only through declared transforms satisfying sink policy.

scope_limit.text: Catching labelled flows at named endpoints does not establish non-interference across the whole graph. General propagation is bounded by what is actually traced, and the registry records that debt rather than hiding it.

reader_ladder.plain: Where a value came from, and how far it is allowed to travel, must follow it everywhere. Untrusted material can only reach a sensitive place after passing through a stated cleaning step.

analogy.text: Allergen information has to follow an ingredient all the way through the kitchen. A clean-looking label on the final plate is not enough if nobody tracked the nuts.

Untrusted material, a prompt, a model-output data, or private-adjacent source, may reach a privileged or public sink only through a declared transform whose output the sink's policy admits. The endpoint cannot certify its own cleanliness: the label has to have been carried, not stamped on at the door. This is why a clean-looking final step is not enough, and why the system tracks how far a value may travel rather than just what it currently looks like.

formal_statement.reads: A derived value carries at least the restriction of what it was derived from; and for any flow into a sink, either the value's label already sits within the sink's policy, or the flow passes through a declared transform whose output label the sink's policy admits. The endpoint never stamps the label; the label arrives with the value.

relationship_triad.requires: A provenance class and ceiling carried with the value, and a declared transform before untrusted material reaches a privileged sink.
relationship_triad.refuses: An endpoint asserting a clean label without that label having propagated.

doctrine_entities.title: Compensable transactional effects
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Effect e requires a compensator or declared irreversible boundary; multi-step effects land as saga with CAS and single-writer constraints.
doctrine_entities.statement: Effect e requires a compensator or declared irreversible boundary; multi-step effects land as saga with CAS and single-writer constraints.

reader_ladder.plain: A change to the world only counts as done if there is a stated way to undo it, or a clear note saying it can never be undone. A multi-step change only goes through if the starting point it expected is still there and nobody else is changing the same thing at the same time.

analogy.text: A money transfer between accounts only completes if the bank can either reverse it or has marked it as final and non-refundable, and a multi-leg transfer only proceeds when the balance it started from has not changed and no second transfer is touching the same account.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: Reading this as a promise that everything is reversible. It actually allows changes to be marked permanently final too; the rule is that the change must declare which one it is, not that undo is always possible.

deep_reading.text: Microcosm treats a write as inadmissible until there is a way back from it or an explicit declaration that there is not. An effect counts as landed only if it carries a compensator that can reverse it or a declared irreversible boundary that marks the point of no return, and a multi-step effect lands as a saga whose every step compares against the head it expected and finds a single writer holding the path. The failure this refuses is the half-completed write: a sequence that succeeds partway, hits a moved head or a second writer, and leaves the world in a state nobody declared and nobody can undo. This ties back to the admissibility floor, because a landing that cannot be recomputed against its expected parent or rolled back is an effect asserting its own success with no check behind it, which is exactly the bare assertion the evidence order puts at the bottom.

formal_statement.reads: An effect may count as landed only if it declares a compensator or an irreversible boundary; and a multi-step effect lands only while the parent it expected still matches the head and at most one writer holds its path. This is where the evidence model meets time: the admissibility floor decides whether a claim counts at all, and this axiom adds that a live claim's strength decays with its own staleness unless its declared basis still holds. It bites hardest on the things that look most authoritative, the running counts and dashboard totals, because those are exactly the values a reader assumes are fresh.

deep_reading.text: AX-11 turns the doctrine itself into something the system can execute rather than merely read. A standard, contract, or rule may carry authority only when an executable grammar accepts its form and it arrives with its result record obligations and its own scope boundary attached; a clause that is only well written sits at the level of a projection, not a law. This is what stops a confident standard from governing by rhetoric: the gate decides on the artifact's checkable shape, not its prose, so the same admissibility discipline AX-1 imposes on claims is imposed on the documents that define how claims are judged. The bite is the second negative case as much as the first: passing the grammar admits the artifact's shape and never certifies that the doctrine it expresses is complete, so a grammar pass that is read as coverage is rejected, not rewarded.

doctrine_entities.summary_line: Echoing a fixture verdict, registry label, markdown claim, or model answer instead of recomputing it from lower-level evidence.
doctrine_entities.statement: Echoing a fixture verdict, registry label, markdown claim, or model answer instead of recomputing it from lower-level evidence.

scope_limit.text: Guarding against label echo is a floor under AX-1 and AX-12, not a positive proof that any specific claim is true.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of repeating a stored verdict, label, or model answer as if it were true, without re-deriving it from the underlying evidence.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a label being present means it was checked. The label is just text until something recomputes the verdict beneath it.

deep_reading.text: AP-1 is the failure AX-1 exists to refuse: taking a declared verdict at face value because it is written down. It is tempting because echoing is cheap and usually looks right, so a pipeline that repeats labels passes its own tests while proving nothing. The repair is not subtle: recompute the verdict from the evidence underneath and keep a negative fixture that fails when the echo is wrong. If you cannot recompute it, the honest output is a lower claim, not a confident repeat.

doctrine_entities.summary_line: Trusting a producer, persona, route, account secret, or prior success instead of a checker, proof, policy, or dereferenced capability.
doctrine_entities.statement: Trusting a producer, persona, route, account secret, or prior success instead of a checker, proof, policy, or dereferenced capability.

scope_limit.text: Refusing producer trust at these witnesses is a floor under AX-2 and AX-3, not positive proof that any granted authority or accepted claim is correct. The example is reader illustration and computes no support; catching identity-based trust in named places does not establish that authority is correctly derived everywhere.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of letting something through because of who sent it, what badge it carries, or that it worked last time, instead of independently checking that this request is actually allowed right now.

analogy.text: A building guard waving someone through to a secure room because their face is familiar and they have an old pass, rather than checking the access system to confirm that person is cleared for that room today.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a familiar face is not the same as a confirmed permission. It does not establish the access system itself is correct, that every door in the building is checked this way, or that a confirmed person will behave well once inside.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: Identity is easy to fake or to go stale; a system that trusts the sender rather than re-checking the request looks fine until that sender is wrong or compromised, and by then nothing was actually guarding the door.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a trusted name or a pass that worked before is a safe stand-in for checking. The check has to be made each time against what is actually allowed now.

deep_reading.text: AP-2 is the failure that AX-2 and AX-3 exist to refuse: granting trust because of who produced a claim or what badge they hold, rather than because something recomputed the claim or derived the authority. It bites because identity is cheap to read and usually correlates with correctness, so a system that trusts a known producer, a passing route, or a standing account secret looks fine right up until that producer is wrong or compromised, at which point nothing was actually checking. The repair splits trust from production: a small checker decides the claim over its certificate, and authority for an effect is derived from dereferenced tokens, policy, and proof references against current world state, never from ambient identity or a prior green run. This is the human-pressure analogue of the label echo in AP-1; here the unchecked thing is a source of authority rather than a written verdict.

scope_limit.text: Refusing rank-as-score does not raise the standing of any part or make the composite correct. It only keeps the number honest as a projection of the ceiling; the parts beneath it carry exactly the support they were already shown to have, and an uncovered part stays blocked rather than counted.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of reading a single summary number, like how many checks passed, as if it told you the whole thing is finished or ready, when parts you never measured could still be failing.

analogy.text: Reading a station board that says forty trains ran on time and concluding the whole network is running well, when several lines simply have no data on the board and could be down.

maps.analogy: the forty-on-time number read as the whole network being fine

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a flattering tally can hide an unmeasured part. It does not establish the lines that do report are running well, and it does not establish anything about lines the board never covered.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: Counting passing checks as a maturity score quietly treats anything unmeasured as if it passed, so a project can look launch-ready while a required piece was never even tested.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That more passing checks always means more readiness. Extra passes only help if they cover a part that had no coverage before; repeating the same passing check adds nothing.

deep_reading.text: AP-3 is the roll-up fallacy the system polices in its own progress reporting: treating a number that summarises many parts as a verdict on the whole. A count of passing checks, a list of registered handles, a green validator, or a strong evidence-class label is a projection over an eight-component ceiling vector, and a high reading on one component can hide an uncovered provenance, freshness, or coverage component underneath it. This bites because it inverts how a composite is supposed to score: the honest status of a whole is the meet of its parts, where any part with no admissible witness sits at blocked, so a flattering average or a raw tally quietly reads a fail-open default as a pass. The repair is the count-theater rule: more passing cases raise standing only by covering a previously uncovered required obligation, lifting a sub-maximal ceiling component, or adding a missing negative case; redundant cases under the same basis are inert, and a rank stays a display of the ceiling, never the authority itself.

formal_statement.reads: Reporting a tally of passing parts as the standing of the whole while some part has no admissible witness, so the claimed status rises above the meet of the parts that an uncovered part should pin to the bottom.

This object and its example are reader illustration; they never count as support or proof that freshness holds across the graph, and the source records the freshness component as an open gap rather than a closed one.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That an unchanged name means unchanged content. The name can stay identical while what it points to has been replaced underneath.

deep_reading.text: AP-4 is the failure the determinism and freshness floors exist to refuse: trusting a stable handle as if it still stood for stable content. It is tempting because the handle does not visibly change when the basis drifts, so a name lookup, a route, or a producer keeps returning yesterday's answer and the pipeline looks fast and consistent while quietly serving a stale value. This connects to the claim and evidence model directly: a cached result is a claim over a basis, and if its basis has moved, the certificate that once admitted it no longer holds, so the value has dropped to bottom evidence even though the label reads unchanged. The repair is content-addressed identity: derive the cache key from a digest of the basis, reuse only when that digest matches, and on drift recompute or refuse rather than serve the old value by its handle.

doctrine_entities.title: Unknown-unknown exhaustiveness
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Treating missing evidence as evidence of absence outside a declared closed domain.
doctrine_entities.statement: Treating missing evidence as evidence of absence outside a declared closed domain.

scope_limit.text: Holding a gap open as unknown does not establish the missing claim either way; it keeps the absence from becoming a false negative, and it grants no support, completeness, or coverage beyond the declared finite domain it names.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of treating a place where you found nothing as a settled finding that nothing is there, when you may simply not have looked, or not looked everywhere.

analogy.text: A doctor reading a region of a scan as 'all clear' when that region was never actually imaged, so 'we saw no problem' gets reported as 'there is no problem'.

maps.doctrine: a missing witness, an evidence gap
maps.analogy: the region of the body that was never imaged

maps.doctrine: reading that gap as a settled negative
maps.analogy: reading the un-imaged region as 'all clear'

maps.doctrine: closing as a negative only inside a declared finite domain where every case is checked
maps.analogy: being able to say 'clear' only for the area actually scanned end to end

analogy.boundary: This shows only that 'we found nothing' is not the same as 'there is nothing'. It does not establish whether the un-imaged region is actually healthy or not, and it does not turn a properly scanned clear area into a guarantee.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: An unexamined gap quietly reads as reassurance, so a coverage map can look finished when it has only stopped looking, hiding risk exactly where no one checked.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a blank or absence is the same as a confirmed 'nothing here'. Absence of evidence is unknown, not a settled negative, unless the whole area was genuinely covered.

deep_reading.text: AP-5 is the failure AX-6 exists to refuse: turning a gap in evidence into a positive verdict of nothing-there. A required obligation with no admissible witness is an open coverage gap, not a refutation; it can be closed as a negative only inside a declared finite domain where every case is enumerable. This bites because it is the comfortable direction to round: a quiet absence reads as reassurance, and a coverage map that prints absent as clear looks finished when it has only stopped looking. It connects to the claim and evidence model through a distinction the system holds by construction: a missing witness is unknown, which is held separate from a value at the bottom of the evidence order, and unknown is kept distinct from a fail-closed block where an in-domain obligation has no admissible witness; collapsing any of these into proven-absent launders an open gap into a certified claim it cannot support.

formal_statement.reads: Reporting the negation of a claim as established while the claim is merely unproven and the domain was never declared finite, so an open gap is laundered into a settled negative.

symbols.meaning: a claim whose proof is missing
reporting the negation as an established finding
an admissible derivation exists for the claim
D is a declared finite domain where closed-world coverage is valid
the domain the reasoning ranges over

relationship_triad.requires: Holding an uncovered obligation as an open gap, and closing it as a negative only inside a declared finite domain.
relationship_triad.refuses: Treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence outside a declared closed domain.

doctrine_entities.title: Inadmissible number emission
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Emitting inadmissible numbers or conclusions instead of typed refusal.
doctrine_entities.statement: Emitting inadmissible numbers or conclusions instead of typed refusal.

scope_limit.text: Refusing one inadmissible emission at a named site does not establish a computation total or its in-domain numbers correct. It keeps the absence of an answer honest; the value it does return is still only as strong as the basis and check beneath it, and this record and its example never count as support for that.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of producing a number anyway when the thing it needs to be valid is missing, instead of clearly saying 'I cannot answer this and here is why'.

analogy.text: A pharmacist guessing and dispensing a dose when the patient's weight, the one input the formula needs, is missing, instead of stopping and saying the dose cannot be worked out yet.

maps.doctrine: a precondition that does not hold
maps.analogy: the missing patient weight the dose formula requires

maps.doctrine: emitting a value anyway to keep going
maps.analogy: guessing and handing over a dose regardless

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a missing input should produce an explicit refusal, not a made-up answer. It does not establish that a dose computed with all the right inputs is correct, and a refusal is not itself a treatment.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: A fabricated number looks just like a real one downstream, so a statistic computed outside its valid range slides into later steps that trust it, while an honest refusal stops the bad value at the door.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That returning some number is more helpful than refusing. A number produced when its inputs are missing is worse than a refusal, because it hides as a usable result.

deep_reading.text: AP-6 is the failure AX-7 exists to refuse: when a computation's precondition does not hold, or a library it needs is absent, the code returns a number anyway instead of a typed refusal that names why it could not answer. It is tempting because a refusal reads as a red path and a number keeps the pipeline green, so a finance statistic computed past its valid sample size, or a silent NaN, slides downstream wearing the same shape as a real result. In the claim model that emitted number is a bare assertion with no admissible basis: it sits at the bottom of the evidence order, but unlike an honest gap it hides as a value later steps will trust. The repair is to totalize the partial function, return Ok only under a declared precondition and otherwise a refusal carrying a reason and the evidence for it, so the absence of an answer becomes a checkable typed object rather than a fabricated one.

formal_statement.reads: The precondition fails, yet the computation emits a value y instead of a refusal carrying a reason and its evidence.

symbols.meaning: the declared precondition the computation needs to hold
emitting the partial computation's value as a result
the partial computation on input x
an emitted number or conclusion
a typed refusal carrying a reason r and evidence e

relationship_triad.governs: The boundary where a partial computation must either answer under its precondition or refuse.
relationship_triad.requires: Catching the inadmissible value: a totalized result that returns Ok only under a declared precondition and otherwise a refusal carrying a reason and evidence.
relationship_triad.refuses: Emitting a meaningless statistic, a silent NaN, or an out-of-domain conclusion just to keep a green path.

example.text: The finance forecast evaluation component returns a typed refusal when a forecast horizon reaches or exceeds the sample size, or when the statistics dependency it needs is unavailable, rather than reporting a number computed outside its valid range.

counterexample.text: A statistics routine returns a coefficient computed past its valid sample size, and a downstream summary reports it as a normal result because it arrived as a number and not as a refusal.

doctrine_entities.title: Public/private membrane breach
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Letting untrusted, private, provider, prompt, account secret, or raw-voice material reach a privileged or public sink without provenance an…
doctrine_entities.statement: Letting untrusted, private, provider, prompt, account secret, or raw-voice material reach a privileged or public sink without provenance and sanitizer transform.

scope_limit.text: Guarding the membrane at named endpoints is a floor under AX-8, not a positive proof of non-interference across the whole graph; endpoint catches are not general propagation, and the example illustrates the boundary rather than computing any support for it.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of letting private or untrusted material reach a public or high-trust place just because the last step looked clean, without a label saying where it came from and without running it through a stated cleaning step first.

analogy.text: Waving a shipment through customs because the final truck looked ordinary, even though no declaration form rode with the goods and no inspection was actually performed.

maps.doctrine: the private or untrusted value entering a flow
maps.analogy: the goods arriving at the border

maps.doctrine: the public or high-trust place it reaches (the sink)
maps.analogy: entry into the country past customs

maps.doctrine: the provenance label that must travel with the value
maps.analogy: the declaration form stating where the goods are from

maps.doctrine: the declared cleaning step the value must pass through
maps.analogy: the actual inspection that clears the goods

maps.doctrine: the clean-looking final step that hides the breach
maps.analogy: the ordinary truck that makes everyone wave it through

analogy.boundary: This shows the crossing must be gated by what travels with the goods, not by how the truck looks; it does not establish that checking goods at one border post keeps every border in the country clean, and one clean shipment does not mean the whole supply chain is safe.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: It is how a system can publish from private-adjacent sources at all without leaking secrets, account secrets, or planted instructions onto a public page.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That if the last copy step looks tidy and nothing obviously private is visible, the material is safe to publish.

deep_reading.text: AP-7 is the failure AX-8 exists to refuse: a value crosses into a public or privileged sink carrying trust it never earned. It bites because the final step usually looks clean, so a pipeline that copies a private-adjacent body, a model-output data, a prompt instruction, or source notes into a published page passes its own checks while leaking, since nothing recomputed where the value came from or what was done to it on the way. The repair follows the boundary model directly: a provenance class and ceiling must travel with the value, and untrusted material may reach the sink only through a declared transform whose output the sink's policy admits, never a clean label stamped on at the door. This is the membrane that lets the system publish from private-adjacent source at all, because the act of crossing is gated by carried provenance rather than by how the endpoint happens to look.

formal_statement.reads: A flow carries x into a sink s while x's carried provenance label sits above what the sink's policy may admit, and the flow passes through no declared sanitizing transform whose output label the sink's policy admits.

symbols.meaning: an untrusted, private, provider, prompt, or raw-voice value entering a flow
a public or privileged sink
x's carried provenance class and ceiling
what the sink is allowed to admit
sits above the ceiling the sink admits
a declared sanitizing transform
T is a declared sanitizing transform whose output the sink's policy admits

relationship_triad.governs: The boundary where material and its trust label cross into a public or privileged sink.
relationship_triad.requires: Carrying a provenance class and ceiling with the value, and routing untrusted material through a declared transform the sink's policy admits before it crosses.
relationship_triad.refuses: Untrusted, private, provider, prompt, account secret, or raw-voice material reaching a privileged or public sink on a clean-looking final step, with no provenance carried and no declared transform applied.

example.text: The prompt-injection replay carries an information-flow policy with the data, so an untrusted instruction arriving at a tool call is caught at the boundary instead of trusted for having reached a trusted endpoint.

counterexample.text: A public page prints a value lifted from a private-adjacent source because the final copy step looked clean, with no provenance carried across the copy and no sanitizing transform between the source and the page.

doctrine_entities.title: Blind irreversible mutation
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Performing irreversible mutation without a compensator, rollback result record, CAS/world-version guard, or explicit irreversible boundary.
doctrine_entities.statement: Performing irreversible mutation without a compensator, rollback result record, CAS/world-version guard, or explicit irreversible boundary.

scope_limit.text: Guarding the named landing paths against blind writes does not establish every effect in the system is reversible or race-free. It holds the specific obligations AX-9 names, compensator-or-boundary, compare-and-swap, single-writer, over the surfaces that bind them, and the example illustrates that floor rather than counting as support for it.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of making a real, hard-to-undo change while assuming it can always be taken back, when nothing was set up to take it back and nothing checked the situation had not already moved.

analogy.text: Sending a bank transfer with no way to recall it and without first checking the account balance had not already changed since you looked.

maps.doctrine: the irreversible effect being written
maps.analogy: the money leaving your account

maps.doctrine: the compensator or declared irreversible boundary
maps.analogy: either a recall option or an upfront note that this transfer cannot be reversed

maps.doctrine: the compare-and-swap check against the expected parent state
maps.analogy: confirming the balance still matches what you saw before you authorise the send

maps.doctrine: two writers racing on the same path
maps.analogy: two people moving money from the same account at once

analogy.boundary: This shows the obligation to set up a recall path and a balance check before sending; it does not establish that every transaction in the bank is reversible or race-free, only that these specific steps were put in place for this send.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: It stops a change from silently overwriting someone else's concurrent work or landing half-done with no recorded way to undo it.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That because the normal case completes fine, you can always undo a change later if something goes wrong.

deep_reading.text: AP-8 is the failure AX-9 exists to refuse: writing a real effect into the world while assuming it can always be taken back, when nothing was put in place to take it back. It bites because the happy path looks identical whether or not a guard exists; the gap only appears when two writers race, a parent state has already moved, or a step half-lands and there is no recorded way to undo it. The repair is to make every effect declare its own reversibility up front: a compensator or an explicitly named irreversible boundary, multi-step effects landing under compare-and-swap against an expected parent, and same-path writes held to a single writer. This connects to the evidence model through provenance and freshness rather than through a label: a write is only safe to treat as landed when the state it assumed is still the state it is acting on, and a record of how to reverse it travels with the effect rather than being assumed after the fact.

formal_statement.reads: An effect e is landed while no compensator reverses it, no irreversible boundary is declared for it, and no compare-and-swap guards it against the parent state having advanced.

symbols.meaning: e is a real effect being written to the world
an effect being written to the world
a compensator that would reverse the effect
c is a compensator that reverses effect e
an explicit declaration that the effect cannot be undone
a compare-and-swap guard checking the parent state has not advanced under e

relationship_triad.governs: The effect boundary, where a mutation is treated as safely landed.
relationship_triad.requires: Catching the blind write: a compensator or a declared irreversible boundary, compare-and-swap against the expected parent for multi-step effects, and a single writer per path.
relationship_triad.refuses: Writing an irreversible effect with no compensator, no rollback record, no compare-and-swap or world-version guard, and no declared irreversible boundary.

example.text: The work-landing replay refuses to advance when the expected parent has moved under it and when the head was not advanced as recorded, so a multi-step effect cannot land blindly over a state that has already changed.

doctrine_entities.title: Frozen live fact
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Freezing live facts in prose without `as_of`, basis, and rederive contract.
doctrine_entities.statement: Freezing live facts in prose without `as_of`, basis, and rederive contract.

scope_limit.text: Blocking unbound live values does not establish a freshness contract is in place everywhere, nor that any carried as-of value is current. It is a floor under AX-10 and P-11; it catches the frozen figure, it does not certify that the figures still bound to a basis are fresh.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of writing a moving number or a 'current' status into permanent text as if it were a fixed fact, with no note of when it was read, what it was read from, and no way to recompute it.

analogy.text: Printing a train's departure time onto a permanent sign instead of leaving it on the live board, so it keeps showing the old time long after the schedule changes.

maps.doctrine: the live value (a count or current state)
maps.analogy: the train's departure time, which keeps changing

maps.doctrine: freezing it into durable prose
maps.analogy: printing it onto a permanent sign

maps.doctrine: the as-of time that should travel with it
maps.analogy: a timestamp saying when this time was accurate

maps.doctrine: the basis it was read from
maps.analogy: the underlying timetable the departure time came from

maps.doctrine: the rederive route that recomputes it
maps.analogy: the live board you could check to get the real current time

analogy.boundary: This shows that a moving value frozen in permanent text drifts while the text stays put; it does not establish that any value left on the live board is itself currently correct, only that a printed sign loses the ability to be re-checked.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: It keeps readers from trusting a stale figure that reads exactly like a live one, long after the real number has moved.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That because the number was true the moment it was written down, it stays a reliable fact afterward.

deep_reading.text: AP-9 is the failure AX-10 exists to refuse: writing a live value into prose as if it were a fixed fact. A count, a "current" total, a readiness signal, or a route tally is a cached read of moving state, so the moment it lands in text without an as-of time, a named basis, and a way to recompute it, the page starts asserting something it can no longer check. It is tempting because the number is true at the instant it is written, and the freshness contract feels like clutter next to a clean figure. The bite is that the value drifts while the prose does not, and a stale figure reads exactly like a live one; under the claim and evidence model the figure has quietly become a bare assertion, admissible only at the bottom of the evidence order because nothing can rederive it. The honest forms are the ones P-11 names: carry the freshness fields, keep the value out of durable prose, or mark it explicitly as a dated snapshot.

formal_statement.latex: \mathrm{durable}(\varphi) \;\wedge\; \mathrm{live}(\varphi) \;\wedge\; \neg\,\exists\, a, b, r.\ \mathrm{carries}(\varphi, \langle a, b, r \rangle)
formal_statement.reads: A live-state value is frozen into durable prose while no as-of time, basis, and rederive route travel with it.

symbols.meaning: a value written into durable text
the value is frozen into durable prose
the value is a read of moving state (a count, a current total, a readiness signal)
the as-of time the read was taken
the basis the value was computed from

relationship_triad.governs: The time-and-freshness boundary, where a moving value is written down as if it were fixed.
relationship_triad.requires: Catching the freeze: a live value must carry an as-of time, a basis, and a rederive route, stay out of durable prose, or be marked a dated snapshot.
relationship_triad.refuses: Freezing a count, a "current" state, or a live total into prose with no as-of, basis, or way to re-derive it.

example.text: The fact-claim audit treats a volatile count written without a freshness contract as a blocking condition rather than a fact, so a frozen live number is caught instead of trusted because it once was true.

counterexample.text: A page states "the system has 77 components" as a flat fact; the figure was right when typed, but nothing records when it was read or how to recompute it, and it keeps reading as current long after it drifts.

doctrine_entities.title: Prose-as-executable-authority
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Granting executable authority to prose doctrine without grammar and result record obligations.
doctrine_entities.statement: Granting executable authority to prose doctrine without grammar and result record obligations.

scope_limit.text: Rejecting prose-as-authority is a floor under AX-11, not a positive proof that any admitted standard is correct or complete. It keeps unparsed prose from governing; a standard that does pass the grammar is still only as strong as the obligations it actually carries, and this example illustrates the rule without counting as support for it.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of treating a confidently written paragraph as a binding rule, when the system never accepted it through its formal checks and it never says what evidence it owes or where it does not apply.

analogy.text: Treating a hand-written 'this person may enter' note taped to a door as real access, when it was never entered into the building's access system and never says which areas or hours it covers.

maps.doctrine: the prose doctrine claiming to govern
maps.analogy: the hand-written note on the door

maps.doctrine: membership in the executable grammar
maps.analogy: being registered in the building's access system

maps.analogy: stating what proof of access it must show

maps.doctrine: the stated scope limit (what it does not establish)
maps.analogy: naming which areas and hours the pass does not cover

analogy.boundary: This shows that an unregistered note is only a readable claim, not real access; it does not establish that a pass which is registered is therefore correct or sufficient, only that an unregistered one should not open doors.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: It stops a pile of confident-sounding paragraphs from accumulating as if they were enforced rules nothing can actually check.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a clearly and authoritatively worded statement is, by virtue of how it reads, a rule the system enforces.

deep_reading.text: AP-10 is the failure AX-11 exists to refuse: letting a sentence govern because it sounds authoritative. A standard, a policy line, or a doctrine page may bind behaviour only when an executable grammar accepts it and it carries result-record obligations and a stated scope limit; prose on its own is a readable view, not a rule. It is tempting because writing a confident paragraph is cheap and reads like governance, so a system accumulates prose that nothing can recompute and mistakes that pile for an enforced contract. The repair is to make the artifact pass the grammar and attach what evidence it must produce and what it does not establish, otherwise holding it at the strength of a projection rather than an authority.

formal_statement.reads: If an artifact is granted governing authority while it is not accepted by the doctrine grammar, or carries no result-record obligations, or carries no scope limit, reject the authority and treat the prose as a projection.

symbols.meaning: a doctrine artifact (standard, policy, page) claiming to govern
d is treated as a binding rule, not a readable view
the language of artifacts the executable doctrine grammar accepts
d declares the result records it must produce
d states its scope limit, what it does not establish

relationship_triad.governs: The boundary between doctrine that governs and prose that only reads as if it does.
relationship_triad.requires: Refusing authority to any doctrine that is not accepted by the grammar or lacks declared result-record obligations and a stated scope limit, holding it as a projection instead.
relationship_triad.refuses: Granting executable authority to prose doctrine without grammar membership, result-record obligations, and a scope limit.

example.text: The executable doctrine grammar accepts a standard as authority only when it parses in the grammar and carries its obligation and scope-limit fields, and keeps a negative case where a prose-only standard that overclaims completeness is rejected rather than admitted.

counterexample.text: A confidently worded policy paragraph is cited as the binding rule for a behaviour, although nothing parses or checks it and it never says what it does not cover.

doctrine_entities.title: Meta-artifact exemption
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Exempting Microcosm's own result records, docs, releases, generated projections, or validators from Microcosm's evidence gates.
doctrine_entities.statement: Exempting Microcosm's own result records, docs, releases, generated projections, or validators from Microcosm's evidence gates.

scope_limit.text: Refusing the meta exemption does not make the system witnessed, complete, or correct. Admission, support, and this refusal are independent; closing the escape hatch only removes the special pleading, and the worked example illustrates the rule without counting as support for any claim that the system actually meets its own floor everywhere.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of letting the system's own pages, checkers, result records, or generated views skip the very evidence test it makes everything else pass, just because it is the system talking about itself.

analogy.text: A testing lab that strictly retests every sample sent in from outside, but lets its own internal samples through on the lab's say-so without running the same test.

analogy.boundary: This shows that the same test must apply to the lab's own samples, removing the self-discount; it does not establish that passing that test makes any sample clean, only that the lab cannot exempt itself from running it.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: It lets the system state its own limits honestly instead of having a flattering self-assessment quietly become a new unchecked claim.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a claim is more trustworthy because the system is reporting on itself, so it deserves a lighter check than outside claims.

deep_reading.text: AP-11 is the escape hatch AX-12 exists to close: a self-claim that gets a discount because the system is talking about itself. It is tempting because the floor is demanding and the meta-layer feels trusted, so a generated page, a validator's own verdict, a result record, or a coverage projection slips through asserting "verified and complete" without passing the admissibility relation it imposes on external work. It bites hardest at the support evaluator, which must itself meet the support floor it computes, and at this very page, which is held below the source it describes and cannot raise that source's authority. The honest move is to route every self-claim through the same gate, so the system can state its own limits without that statement quietly becoming a new unchecked claim.

relationship_triad.requires: Routing every self-claim, in a page, validator, result record, or projection, through the same admissibility and refusal floor imposed on external claims.
relationship_triad.refuses: A self-assessment of verified, complete, or launch-ready that would never pass the floor the system applies to the work it audits.

doctrine_entities.title: Synthetic system substitution
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Using synthetic fixtures as substitutes for available system.
doctrine_entities.statement: Using synthetic fixtures as substitutes for available system.

scope_limit.text: Refusing synthetic substitution does not make the real basis correct, complete, or strong, and it does not forbid synthetic fixtures where they are declared as such. It only stops a fabricated input from carrying a real basis's weight; this example is reader illustration and never counts as support for the rule.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of building a real conclusion on a made-up stand-in input when genuine, shareable material was right there to use, so the fake input quietly lends the conclusion strength it never earned.

analogy.text: A lab keeps a bag of practice 'dummy' blood for training, but when a real patient test is needed the technician uses a dummy bag instead of the available real sample and reports the result as a genuine reading.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: Readers can tell whether a stated result rests on something real and shareable or on a convenient placeholder, so they can judge how much to lean on it.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a stand-in is fine because it looks identical to the real thing on the page. The tempting wrong belief is that looking the same means it can carry the same weight.

deep_reading.text: AP-12 is the failure AX-1, AX-4, and AX-8 jointly refuse: substituting a synthetic fixture for available real material and then letting a real claim ride on it. A synthetic stand-in has no derivation from anything real (so AX-1's checker has nothing to recompute), it is not the content hash of any real basis (so AX-4 cannot tell when it has drifted from the thing it stands for), and it carries no real provenance (so AX-8's label is fabricated at the door rather than propagated). It is tempting because a synthetic fixture is convenient and looks identical to a real one on the page, and the system itself admits synthetic fixtures for shape and negative cases; the line AP-12 polices is narrower, when real material exists, a synthetic substitute must not silently inherit a real basis's strength.

formal_statement.reads: A claim is grounded on a synthetic basis while a real basis was available, the stand-in's content hash differs from the real basis's hash (it was not derived from the real material), and the claim is still allowed to carry more than bottom strength.

doctrine_entities.title: Generated-result record source inversion
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Treating generated result records as hand-authored source.
doctrine_entities.statement: Treating generated result records as hand-authored source.

scope_limit.text: Keeping generated records bound to their basis does not make either the record or the source correct, and this example illustrates the rule without supporting it. Refusing the inversion only preserves lineage; it does not establish that the basis it points back to is itself true or complete.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of treating an auto-generated summary record as if it were the hand-written original, then editing or quoting that summary as the source while the real source it was built from is left behind and no longer matches.

analogy.text: Scribbling a correction onto a library's catalogue card and then citing the card as the book, when the card was only ever copied from the book and the book itself still says something different.

maps.analogy: the catalogue card copied from the book

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a copied card must stay below the book and be redone from it, never used as the origin; it stops there and does not establish that the book itself is correct or up to date.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: It keeps a generated view from quietly outranking the thing it was built from, so a reader knows which artifact is the real origin and which is just a downstream copy.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That whichever copy is already sitting in front of you, with a confident verdict on it, is the thing to edit and cite. The tempting wrong belief is that the handy artifact is the source.

deep_reading.text: AP-13 is the lineage confusion that AX-4 and AX-11 exist to refuse: mistaking a generated result record for the hand-authored source it was derived from. A generated record is a function of a basis, so its identity is the hash of that basis, and its authority can never exceed the basis it recomputes from; the moment it is read as source, it is cut loose from that basis, so drift no longer forces a recompute and a hand-edit to the record becomes an orphan with nothing underneath it. It is tempting because a generated record often looks authored, carries a confident verdict, and is the artifact already on disk, so the cheaper move is to cite it or edit it in place rather than fix the source and regenerate. The repair is to keep the kinds apart by construction: source is hand-authored and content-addresses its outputs, a generated record stays below its basis and is rebuilt from it, and a parity check refuses the record whenever it has drifted from the source it claims to project.

formal_statement.reads: A generated artifact, derived from a basis by a builder, is rejected when it is treated as if it were hand-authored source.

a generated artifact such as a result record or projection
the generator from basis to artifact
the content basis r is derived from

relationship_triad.requires: Keeping a generated record bound to its basis by hash and rebuilt from source, so it is recomputed rather than edited or cited as origin.
relationship_triad.refuses: Treating a generated result record as hand-authored source.

doctrine_entities.statement: Letting public docs imply a hosted service, external service access, source-file mutation, financial or trading decisions, deployment posture, affiliation or endorsement, or whole-system equivalence that no admissible witness backs.

scope_limit.text: Blocking inflated public-authority language does not establish that any specific authority is in fact held; it only refuses the unbacked implication. The example is reader illustration and never counts as support that the system is hosted, deployed, affiliated, or deployment-posture.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of letting a public page's wording imply powers the system does not have, such as being a hosted, ready product, having an outside partner, changing its own source, making financial decisions, or being the same thing as the larger source system, when nothing behind the page backs any of that.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a label must not promise a status nothing backs; it does not say the prototype is bad, and removing the inflated label does not settle whether the system could be deployed either way.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: A reader can trust that what a public page says about itself, like being hosted or ready or affiliated, is limited to what the system can actually back, not free-floating prose.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That impressive-sounding wording is harmless because it costs nothing and usually looks right. The tempting wrong belief is that stating a power is the same as holding it.

deep_reading.text: AP-14 is the inflation the evidence floor exists to refuse: a public page quietly granting itself an authority it cannot back. The danger is that all seven implied authorities (a hosted service, access to an external service, permission to mutate the source, financial or trading decisions, deployment posture, an affiliation or endorsement, or equivalence with the whole private system) are stated for free in prose, while the witness that would actually hold each one is absent. The failure is the unbacked implication, not the implication itself: a backed authority may be stated at its bounded scope. It bites across three floors at once: AX-5, because an in-scope claim with no admissible witness must fail closed rather than read as granted; AX-8, because a public-authority implication is private-adjacent material that may reach a public sink only through a declared transform, not by being asserted at the page; and AX-12, because the system's own copy is held to the same evidence floor it imposes on any other work. The repair is to state only the authority a witness backs, and to demote or refuse the public claim the moment the witness is missing.

formal_statement.reads: If a public artifact lets a reader infer an authority from the inflated set and no admissible witness backs that authority, the claim is demoted to its bounded scope or refused. The bad thing is the unbacked implication, not implication itself.

doctrine_entities.summary_line: Displaying a declared, inferred, or generated downstream target as an observed runtime effect without evidence of the effect relation.
doctrine_entities.statement: Displaying a declared, inferred, or generated downstream target as an observed runtime effect without evidence of the effect relation.

scope_limit.text: Catching one inflated receiver display is a floor under AX-8 and AX-12, not a positive proof that any effect was achieved. Observing the relation at named receivers does not establish that every declared effect downstream held; the unobserved targets stay marked, not blessed.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of showing an action's intended destination as if the action had already landed there, when nothing has actually checked that it reached the receiving end.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that arrival must be confirmed at the receiving end before it is displayed as done; confirming one parcel's arrival does not establish that every parcel that went out arrived, and it does not say the address was the right one.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That because the destination is known in advance, showing it as reached is as good as confirming it. The tempting wrong belief is that knowing where something is headed is the same as seeing it arrive.

deep_reading.text: AP-16 is the failure AX-8 exists to refuse, applied to effects rather than labels: presenting the intended receiver of an action as if it were the witnessed result. A pipeline declares that a value reached a sink, that a write landed in memory, or that a route was taken, and the page renders that declared target as an observed runtime effect, when nothing carried the effect relation across the steps between source and receiver. It is tempting because the downstream target is usually known in advance, so showing it costs nothing and almost always looks right, while the gap between an intended reach and a witnessed one is invisible to a reader. The repair is the same shape AX-8 imposes on provenance: the effect relation has to be carried and observed at the receiver, not asserted from the sending side, and absent that witness the honest display is a declared target marked as unobserved, held below the strength a real observation would carry.

public_glossary.label: Plectis
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Plectis is this project's declared public name. The name does not define a general category or imply affiliation, endorsement, or identity with similarly named external entities.
public_glossary.short_definition: Plectis is this project's public name, covering its mathematical research, formal proofs, and supporting software.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Plectis is this project's public name, covering its mathematical research, formal proofs, and supporting software.
public_glossary.card_definition: The website connects papers and working records with Lean source, reusable software components, and checks. It aims to make both the results and the process accessible for inspection and further work.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Each paper or component has its own scope and evidence status.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The project name is not a certification that every question is solved or every mechanism is complete. Some older technical identifiers retain the name Microcosm for compatibility with earlier files and links.
public_glossary.scope_note: Plectis is the name used on this site and on the public repository. A reader meets it on every page and on the source and licence page.
public_glossary.example: The "Source and licence" page presents Plectis as the public identity over the published, source-open repository, alongside the licence and the naming lineage from Microcosm.

example_route.label: Source & license
example_route.gloss: see the public identity and the open source repository it names

public_glossary.non_example: Do not use Plectis as proof that package ids, old URLs, or source paths were already renamed; the name is the public identity only, and the earlier Microcosm name still lives on in those technical surfaces.

relationships.gloss: Plectis is the current human-facing public label; Microcosm remains a historical and technical compatibility label.
The Plectis name is governed through the existing Plectis/Microcosm standard while compatibility identifiers remain supported.
Cold readers should see Plectis as the public name while still resolving Microcosm compatibility identifiers.
Plectis identity claims must be checked against current source, generated projections, and release gates.

source_refs.gloss: Machine-readable authority for the Plectis public name and Microcosm compatibility boundary.
Doctrine roof for the source-open substrate now presented publicly as Plectis.
Curated landing surface where the human-visible public name is published.

public_glossary.label: component
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Component means one governed public system object in Plectis. It does not claim that every software, physical, or organizational component has this record shape.
public_glossary.short_definition: A component is a distinct part of a system with a defined job and interfaces to other parts.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A component is a distinct part of a system with a defined job and interfaces to other parts.
public_glossary.card_definition: Plectis presents public components with their inputs, outputs, source, and checks. This lets a reader inspect one mechanism without first understanding the entire system.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The component's description should make clear which behaviour it implements and tests.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Combining components can introduce additional interactions. Evidence for each part helps assess the combination, but the combined behaviour may require its own checks and an explanation of how the parts fit together.
public_glossary.scope_note: Component covers the reader-facing units that make up the system, encountered across the public site wherever a unit is named, carded, or linked, with the full set gathered on the components page.
public_glossary.example: The Cold Reader Route Map is one component: a single unit whose job is to lay out a route through the system for someone arriving without prior context, shown on its own card with its evidence line and source route.

example_route.label: Cold Reader Route Map
example_route.gloss: open one live component card

public_glossary.non_example: A component is not a marketing feature and not the whole system in miniature. It is a single unit of running code with a stated boundary, and the public word does not mean every underlying source identifier has been renamed from organ.

relationships.gloss: Components are the public object units exposed by Plectis.
Component is the public copy translation for legacy Microcosm object vocabulary.
Each component needs an explicit limit on what its evidence supports.

source_refs.gloss: Public-site builder translates source object vocabulary into component-facing copy.
Current source atlas still carries legacy object ids.

public_glossary.label: scope limit
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A scope limit is a stated boundary of a claim, permission, or task. On component cards it chiefly identifies what the evidence supports; that use should not be confused with broader release authority.
public_glossary.short_definition: A scope limit states where a claim, permission, or piece of evidence stops applying.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A scope limit states where a claim, permission, or piece of evidence stops applying.
public_glossary.card_definition: For a component, it may restrict the supported inputs, checked behaviour, or conclusions allowed from a result. For mathematical work, it may identify a finite range or an unresolved hypothesis.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The limit should name the actual boundary rather than offer a generic disclaimer.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For example, a recorded test can establish that a specific forged note was rejected. That does not by itself establish that every forgery or every misleading report would be detected.
public_glossary.scope_note: Scope limits appear wherever a result, component card, digest row, evidence page, or agent answer separates what is shown from what is not shown. The same boundary is recorded in source identifiers as a claim ceiling or authority ceiling.
public_glossary.example: The doctrine card "Bind authority to transaction scope" is a scope limit in action: a unit's authority is tied to the bounded transaction it ran, so its claim cannot extend past what that transaction actually covered.

example_route.label: Bind authority to transaction scope
example_route.gloss: open the doctrine card that ties a claim to its bounded scope

public_glossary.non_example: A scope limit is not a flaw, a hedge, or an admission that a result is weak. It is the precise statement of how far one verified result reaches, leaving everything outside that line unclaimed rather than quietly assumed.

relationships.gloss: Each component carries a scope limit.
Public Plectis copy stays honest by keeping scope limits close to evidence.
A scope limit must be read against current public records, not stale memory.

source_refs.gloss: Builder emits scope-limit copy, claim-ceiling index, and canonical question routes.
Component records carry per-object boundary fields consumed by public projections.

public_glossary.label: evidence class
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: An evidence class fixes what kind of support a record provides and which inferences it licenses; it is not a confidence score or a declaration that the underlying claim is true.
public_glossary.short_definition: An evidence class identifies how a claim is supported, such as by a proof, test run, calculation, or citation.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An evidence class identifies how a claim is supported, such as by a proof, test run, calculation, or citation.
public_glossary.card_definition: The classification helps readers distinguish what has actually been checked from what has been inferred or proposed. Each class comes with its own assumptions and limits.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The class must match the evidence attached to the particular claim.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For example, exact arithmetic avoids rounding error in a calculation but does not automatically cover infinitely many cases. A formal proof can cover all cases in its statement while still depending on explicit hypotheses.
public_glossary.scope_note: Evidence class covers the typed backing attached to public results, cards, and packets. A reader meets it on result and component pages where a claim is shown alongside the category of support that stands behind it, and most directly on the evidence page that sets out what a pass proves.
public_glossary.example: On the evidence page, a result marked as fixture-backed carries the fixture-pass evidence class: its support is a test fixture that ran and passed, which is a different and narrower kind of backing than a row linked directly to a source file.

example_route.label: What the pass proves (evidence)
example_route.gloss: see results sorted by the kind of support behind them

public_glossary.non_example: An evidence class is not a quality score or a rank that makes one result better than another, and a high or strong-sounding class is not proof of launch readiness, security, or whole-system correctness. It names the kind of support, not a verdict.

relationships.gloss: Evidence type must be read with the claim boundary.
A record can carry an evidence class describing the support it contains.
Plectis public copy uses evidence classes to avoid overclaiming.

source_refs.gloss: Source registry for component evidence classes.
Builds evidence labels, ranks, profiles, and claim-ceiling routes into the public site.

public_glossary.label: record
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Record means a governed stored result or receipt in this system. It does not by itself carry legal-record status, evidentiary sufficiency, or truth authority.
public_glossary.short_definition: A record is stored information about an object, event, decision, or result.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A record is stored information about an object, event, decision, or result.
public_glossary.card_definition: In Plectis it may be a structured row, file, or packet that can be reopened after a session ends. Its fields should make clear what it describes and where the information came from.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Different records have different authority and evidence roles.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A result record may describe one test run, while a registry record defines an object's identity. Keeping those roles clear prevents a summary of an action from being confused with the source or execution evidence behind it.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers concrete source and generated artifacts across the site: result rows, receipts, generated JSON outputs, review packets, ledgers, and verification entries. A reader meets records wherever a page links out to something inspectable rather than describing it in prose.
public_glossary.example: The doctrine card "Generated-result record source inversion" concerns exactly this: a generated record, such as a result file emitted by a tool, must stay subordinate to the source that produced it rather than being treated as the authority itself.

example_route.label: Generated-result record source inversion
example_route.gloss: open a rule about how generated records relate to their source

public_glossary.non_example: Recording an assertion preserves it for inspection; the act of recording does not make the assertion true.

relationships.gloss: A record can name the support type behind it.
A record's claim boundary must travel with it.
A generated record is not stronger than its source authority.

source_refs.gloss: Generated public index of components, paper modules, glossary terms, and evidence profiles.
Builds public records from source rows and generated projections.

public_glossary.label: substrate
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Substrate means the live files, records, or runtime state on which this system operates. It is a local systems metaphor, not a biological, chemical, or philosophical substrate claim.
public_glossary.short_definition: Here, substrate means the underlying files, stored state, and tools on which the system operates.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Here, substrate means the underlying files, stored state, and tools on which the system operates.
public_glossary.card_definition: It includes the concrete material an agent can inspect or change, beneath the pages and summaries that describe it. Plectis uses the term when distinguishing direct access to working material from access to a copied explanation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The source's role determines what it can authoritatively establish.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A webpage can accurately describe a file without granting access to that file or permission to change it. Type A and Type B describe this access distinction in the project's actor vocabulary.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the source layer of the whole system: files, standards, ledgers, recorded state, and tooling. A reader meets it wherever the pages distinguish the generated public view from the source it was derived from.
public_glossary.example: The Source and license page is the entry point into this substrate, opening onto the source files and records that the rest of the site is generated from.

example_route.label: Source & license
example_route.gloss: open the source layer the pages are generated from

public_glossary.non_example: A substrate is not a vague word for the whole project, and not a mystical layer behind it. It is the specific, inspectable set of files and records that the pages are generated from.

relationships.gloss: Source authority rests in substrate-owned records and tools.
Plectis is a public map over source substrate.
A record is one inspectable artifact inside or generated from substrate.

source_refs.gloss: Doctrine roof for the source-open substrate concept.
Type A operating seed that distinguishes live substrate from chat.

public_glossary.label: source authority
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Source authority means the local source-of-record relationship for a claim or artifact. It does not imply institutional, legal, academic, or moral authority.
public_glossary.short_definition: Source authority identifies which record or implementation controls a particular fact when other views disagree.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Source authority identifies which record or implementation controls a particular fact when other views disagree.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, a registry may define an object's identity, while an execution record describes a run and source code defines an implementation. A generated page presents selected information from those sources.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Authority is specific to the question; one artifact does not settle every kind of claim.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Plectis preserves these distinctions so a convenient summary cannot silently override its inputs. Resolving a mismatch requires identifying the relevant owner and checking what the source actually establishes.
public_glossary.scope_note: Source authority appears wherever a public page describes itself as a map, projection, record, or digest, and points to the underlying file, standard, validator, or ledger that holds the fact. It marks the boundary between a generated surface and the material it is drawn from.
public_glossary.example: The vocabulary registry standard is a source authority: a glossary row on this site can cite it for the meaning of a term while the row itself remains a projection that owns nothing.

example_route.label: Generated-result record source inversion
example_route.gloss: open the anti-pattern that fires when a generated record is mistaken for the source that owns the fact

public_glossary.non_example: Source authority is not a generated page, a digest, or an AI answer. Those are projections; they hold authority only when a governing standard explicitly names them as the owner of the fact.

relationships.gloss: Records point to the authority that owns their claim.
Plectis public pages stay below source authority.
Authority and scope must be named together for public claims.

source_refs.gloss: Defines system vocabulary rows as projections below cited source authority.
Emits source refs and authority boundaries into public packets.

public_glossary.label: organ (source identifier)
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Organ is a retained source/storage compatibility identifier. It is not the preferred public object name, a biological claim, or proof that a storage rename has completed.
public_glossary.short_definition: Organ is the source-code term for a bounded unit that the public site usually calls a component.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Organ is the source-code term for a bounded unit that the public site usually calls a component.
public_glossary.card_definition: It may appear in registry names and paths retained by the implementation. Each unit has a particular job, interfaces, and evidence describing its behaviour.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The biological word is internal terminology; it does not add a separate guarantee or capability.
public_glossary.deep_definition: When following a component card into source code, an organ identifier can refer to that same unit. The registry and linked source establish the identity and scope more precisely than the choice of label.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers every bounded unit the system is assembled from. A reader meets it in source paths and identifiers such as organ_registry.json, and meets the same units as components throughout the public pages, where each can be opened on its own.
public_glossary.example: A concrete organ is the Source Projection Import Protocol, a unit that brings source material across into the public slice; it is listed and openable among the components.

example_route.label: Source Projection Import Protocol
example_route.gloss: browse the units, each openable on its own

public_glossary.non_example: An organ is not a biological metaphor and not a marketing feature. It is a unit of running code with a stated boundary.

relationships.gloss: Component is the preferred reader-facing word.
Organ ids may appear in the public source slice.
Source-level organ records still need claim boundaries.

source_refs.gloss: Source-level registry that still uses organ ids.
Source atlas consumed by public component projections.

public_glossary.label: check result
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In mathematics a witness is an object satisfying an existence claim. In Plectis software records the word can instead identify captured evidence of a check; the two uses have different evidence requirements.
public_glossary.short_definition: A mathematical witness is an object showing that an existence claim holds; in Plectis's software records, the word can also mean evidence of a check.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A mathematical witness is an object showing that an existence claim holds; in Plectis's software records, the word can also mean evidence of a check.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, n = 3 witnesses that some positive integer has square 9. A software witness may instead be a saved verification record tied to a particular execution.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The surrounding claim determines which kind of witness is required.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Supplying an object is useful only when it satisfies the claimed property. Likewise, a record supports an execution claim only within what its source and recording process can establish.

public_glossary.label: navigable
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Navigable means a cold reader can discover, select, open, and verify an artifact through supported routes; it is stronger than merely being searchable or linked somewhere.
public_glossary.short_definition: Material is navigable when a reader has usable routes from its summary to the relevant detail or next action.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Material is navigable when a reader has usable routes from its summary to the relevant detail or next action.

public_glossary.label: 2-kernel
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The 2-kernel is a family of subsequences. It is distinct from a null space, a software core, or Lean’s proof-checking kernel.
public_glossary.short_definition: The 2-kernel of a sequence a(n) is the family of subsequences n↦a(2ᵉn+r), for all e≥0 and 0≤r<2ᵉ.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The 2-kernel of a sequence a(n) is the family of subsequences n↦a(2ᵉn+r), for all e≥0 and 0≤r<2ᵉ.
public_glossary.card_definition: At level e, the original sequence is split by residue classes modulo 2ᵉ. For e=1 these are the even-indexed and odd-indexed subsequences; higher levels repeatedly split each section.
public_glossary.reader_rule: This “kernel” is a family of sequences, not a null space, software core, or proof checker. A sequence is 2-automatic or 2-regular under additional finiteness conditions on the states or module generated by this family.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The paper constructs a rational basis and exact finite-level ranks for the dyadic sections of Euler’s totient. Its headline “2-kernel” refers precisely to this collection across all levels.
public_glossary.scope_note: This “kernel” is a family of sequences, not a null space, software core, or proof checker. A sequence is 2-automatic or 2-regular under additional finiteness conditions on the states or module generated by this family.
public_glossary.example: At level e, the original sequence is split by residue classes modulo 2ᵉ.

public_glossary.label: above and beyond
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Inside ai_workflow this means bounded durable follow-through, not overwork, speculative expansion, or permission to exceed the user's scope.
public_glossary.short_definition: In Plectis, “above and beyond” means doing the useful follow-through that makes a completed task easy to find, check, and continue.
public_glossary.reader_preview: In Plectis, “above and beyond” means doing the useful follow-through that makes a completed task easy to find, check, and continue.
public_glossary.card_definition: Finishing a change can leave a broken link, an outdated instruction, or a lesson that exists only in the conversation. This term asks the agent to fix the directly related loose ends while the context is still available.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The extra work needs a clear stopping point and must fit the user's authorised scope.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For example, a new feature may need its existing guide updated and its check recorded so the next person can use it.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers how a unit of work is judged complete across the system, and it appears wherever a pass reports what it finished and what it deliberately left for later, most directly on the surfaces that audit whether a pass closed its loop honestly.
public_glossary.example: The Agent Completion Faithfulness Audit is a concrete instance: it is the check that compares what a pass claims it finished against what it actually closed, which is the boundary that above and beyond stays inside.

public_glossary.label: absolute convergence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A series converges absolutely if the sum of the absolute values of its terms is finite.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A series converges absolutely if the sum of the absolute values of its terms is finite.
public_glossary.card_definition: For a real or complex series ∑ aₙ, this means ∑ |aₙ| converges. It implies convergence of the original series and permits rearranging its terms without changing the sum.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Ordinary convergence does not imply absolute convergence: the alternating harmonic series is a standard counterexample.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For nonnegative terms, the two conditions coincide. Absolute convergence is useful in the papers when expanding denominators, regrouping contributions, or bounding an omitted tail by the sum of its magnitudes.
public_glossary.scope_note: Ordinary convergence does not imply absolute convergence: the alternating harmonic series is a standard counterexample.

public_glossary.label: absolute value
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Real and complex numbers. For vectors and functions the analogous object is usually called a norm.
public_glossary.short_definition: A number's nonnegative size, ignoring sign; for complex numbers it is distance from zero.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A number's nonnegative size, ignoring sign; for complex numbers it is distance from zero.
public_glossary.card_definition: Absolute value measures size without sign. Thus |-3|=3, while for the complex number z=3+4i, |z|=5 because the point (3,4) lies five units from the origin. It is zero only at zero.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The distance between real or complex numbers x and y is |x−y|. Products satisfy |xy|=|x||y|, and sums satisfy the triangle inequality |x+y|≤|x|+|y|; cancellation can make the left side much smaller.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In these papers absolute values measure approximation errors, bound nonzero integer expressions from below, and define polynomial regions such as {|f(z)|<1}. For vectors or functions, the related size concept usually needs a separately specified norm.
public_glossary.scope_note: The distance between real or complex numbers x and y is |x−y|. Products satisfy |xy|=|x||y|, and sums satisfy the triangle inequality |x+y|≤|x|+|y|; cancellation can make the left side much smaller.
