public_glossary.label: derivation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A derivation is a sequence of justified steps leading from stated starting points to a result.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A derivation is a sequence of justified steps leading from stated starting points to a result.
public_glossary.card_definition: In mathematics, the steps use definitions, assumptions, and valid inference rules. In the software descriptions, a derivation can instead describe how a generated object was obtained from its sources.

public_glossary.label: deterministic
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A deterministic process produces the same output whenever all relevant inputs and operating conditions are the same.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A deterministic process produces the same output whenever all relevant inputs and operating conditions are the same.
public_glossary.card_definition: Determinism rules out unresolved random choice for a fixed execution state. Reproducibility still depends on treating versions, ordering, clocks, external responses, and configuration as inputs when they can affect the result.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The same specified input and environment determine one output; any random seed, time value, scheduling order, or external response that affects execution belongs among those conditions.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A deterministic algorithm maps each complete input state to one result. Running it twice with truly identical inputs therefore gives identical output. Apparent exceptions often come from hidden inputs: system time, directory order, concurrent scheduling, floating-point platform details, network responses, tool versions, or an unrecorded random seed. Determinism does not establish correctness, speed, or real-world validity; a consistently wrong calculation is still deterministic. It also differs from reproducibility, which asks whether another execution environment can reconstruct the conditions closely enough to obtain the recorded result.
public_glossary.scope_note: Deterministic applies to the named process under its declared inputs, versions, and environment.
public_glossary.example: Generating the glossary twice from the same registry and builder revision should produce byte-identical output.
public_glossary.non_example: A process is not deterministic merely because two observed runs happened to agree.

public_glossary.label: Diebold-Mariano test
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The Diebold–Mariano test assesses whether two forecasting methods have equal expected loss under a chosen measure of error.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The Diebold–Mariano test assesses whether two forecasting methods have equal expected loss under a chosen measure of error.
public_glossary.card_definition: It compares the loss differences between paired forecasts and accounts for time dependence through an estimate of their long-run variance. Squared error and absolute error can lead to different comparisons.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Interpret the result under the test's sampling and dependence assumptions.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The test addresses average predictive loss in the analysed setting. Statistical significance neither identifies the cause of a difference nor guarantees that the better-performing method will remain better on future data.
public_glossary.scope_note: Named for Francis Diebold and Roberto Mariano; the test is standard in forecast evaluation and is not a contribution of this work.

public_glossary.label: differentiable function
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: This entry concerns mathematical differentiability, not whether two data records can be distinguished.
public_glossary.short_definition: A function with a linear first-order approximation at each point under discussion.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A function with a linear first-order approximation at each point under discussion.
public_glossary.card_definition: The derivative gives a linear approximation whose error becomes negligible compared with the change in input. Squaring is differentiable everywhere on the reals; absolute value is continuous at zero but has no derivative there because its two one-sided slopes disagree.
public_glossary.reader_rule: In several variables use the full linear approximation, not merely the existence of all partial derivatives; in complex analysis complex differentiability is substantially stronger than real differentiability.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For a real function of one variable, differentiability at x means that the difference quotient approaches a finite limit. In several real variables, differentiability means there is a linear map that approximates the increment with an error small compared with the increment's size. For a curve z(t), its derivative is its instantaneous velocity. For complex functions, the same quotient must have one limit independent of the direction of approach; differentiability on an open set then leads to holomorphicity. Differentiability implies continuity at the point, but continuity alone does not imply differentiability.
public_glossary.scope_note: In several variables use the full linear approximation, not merely the existence of all partial derivatives; in complex analysis complex differentiability is substantially stronger than real differentiability.
public_glossary.example: The trajectory assumption z'(t)=N(z(t)) in the Newton-flow paper requires z to be differentiable in the time parameter.
public_glossary.non_example: Having directional or coordinate partial derivatives alone does not guarantee differentiability in several variables.

public_glossary.label: digest

public_glossary.reader_preview: A cryptographic digest is a fixed-size value computed from data, used to detect whether the data has changed.
public_glossary.card_definition: The same bytes produce the same digest under the same algorithm. Plectis uses hashes to connect generated material and result records to particular file contents.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A mismatch proves the contents differ; a matching secure hash provides strong practical evidence of equality.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Different inputs can theoretically share a digest, so it is not a mathematical guarantee of identical bytes. A digest also says nothing about the truth or quality of the contents.

public_glossary.label: digestion
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The staged meaning of digestion used here is Terence Tao's, from Mathematics in the age of AI (arXiv:2608.16753). This site does not own or redefine that stage; it only says how it tries to help authors assist it. Community digestion and acceptance remain external.
public_glossary.short_definition: Mathematical digestion is the process of understanding a result well enough to place it in the field and use it in further work.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Mathematical digestion is the process of understanding a result well enough to place it in the field and use it in further work.
public_glossary.card_definition: It includes identifying the main idea, checking how the hypotheses matter, connecting the result to earlier work, and finding useful applications or reformulations. The site's discussion follows the distinction between verifying a proof and making its mathematics usable.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A checked proof and a published paper can support this process without completing it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Clear explanations, failed approaches, and precise open questions help other mathematicians assess and continue the work. Community uptake cannot be awarded by a repository's own checks.
public_glossary.scope_note: The word is Tao's. The local use is: keep the record that would help a mathematician digest the work. The local use is not: declare the work digested.

public_glossary.non_example: A long formally verified proof with no account of the hard step, the false starts, or what remains open is not digestion, however correct it is.

public_glossary.label: dimension
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Linear algebra. Distinct from geometric fractal dimension or software array dimensions.
public_glossary.short_definition: A vector space has dimension equal to the size of a basis; geometric notions such as Hausdorff dimension use different definitions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A vector space has dimension equal to the size of a basis; geometric notions such as Hausdorff dimension use different definitions.
public_glossary.card_definition: The ordinary plane has vector-space dimension two because every vector has a unique expression using two independent coordinate directions. A line through the origin has dimension one, while a space of all infinite sequences can be infinite-dimensional.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Linear dimension is the size of a basis over a specified scalar field. Showing independent families of every finite size proves infinite-dimensionality. It does not mean each individual vector has infinitely many geometric directions.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The arithmetic-function papers prove large or infinite linear dimension using evaluation matrices and independent channel families. Geometric notions such as Hausdorff dimension answer a different covering-scale question, so the qualifying word determines which definition applies.

public_glossary.label: dirichlet convolution
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Arithmetic functions. The manuscript may say divisor transform without naming convolution.
public_glossary.short_definition: The arithmetic-function product (f*g)(n)=Σ_{d|n}f(d)g(n/d).
public_glossary.reader_preview: The arithmetic-function product (f*g)(n)=Σ_{d|n}f(d)g(n/d).
public_glossary.card_definition: For arithmetic functions f and g, their Dirichlet convolution at a positive integer n is the sum of f(d)g(n/d) over positive divisors d of n. If both functions equal 1, the result counts divisors: for n = 6 it counts 1, 2, 3, and 6.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The summation runs over divisors d of n and pairs each with n/d. This is not ordinary additive convolution, which sums over decompositions such as a+b=n. The identity element is 1 at n=1 and 0 elsewhere.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Divisor transforms in the Mersenne and totient work reorganize coefficient sequences according to shared factors. Möbius inversion works because the Möbius function is the Dirichlet-convolution inverse of the constant-one function.
public_glossary.scope_note: The summation runs over divisors d of n and pairs each with n/d. This is not ordinary additive convolution, which sums over decompositions such as a+b=n. The identity element is 1 at n=1 and 0 elsewhere.

public_glossary.label: Dirichlet energy
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Finite Dirichlet energy bounds an integral of squared derivatives. It does not by itself bound the derivative at each point.
public_glossary.short_definition: The Dirichlet energy of a sufficiently regular function u on a region is the integral of |∇u|²; for complex maps it measures the total squared stretching.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The Dirichlet energy of a sufficiently regular function u on a region is the integral of |∇u|²; for complex maps it measures the total squared stretching.
public_glossary.card_definition: A constant function has zero energy. A rapidly varying function costs more because its gradient is larger. For a conformal map in the plane, energy is closely related to the area of the image, with conventions sometimes introducing a factor of two.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The normalization and whether u is real-, vector-, or complex-valued must be stated. Finite energy is an averaged square-derivative condition; it does not by itself bound the derivative at every point.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Here the energy of a holomorphic inverse branch controls coefficients and, through Cauchy–Schwarz, the length or diameter of selected traces. It supplies an integral geometric budget rather than a pointwise path bound.

public_glossary.label: dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions
public_glossary.preferred_label: dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Analytic number theory. Distinct from Dirichlet convolution and other theorems named for Dirichlet.
public_glossary.public_phrase: dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions
public_glossary.short_definition: Dirichlet’s theorem says that every residue class a modulo a positive integer q with gcd(a,q) = 1 contains infinitely many primes.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Dirichlet’s theorem says that every residue class a modulo a positive integer q with gcd(a,q) = 1 contains infinitely many primes.
public_glossary.card_definition: Dirichlet’s theorem guarantees infinitely many primes in every arithmetic progression a,a+q,a+2q,… when a and q are coprime. Thus both 1,5,9,… and 3,7,11,… contain infinitely many primes for modulus 4.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The coprimality condition gcd(a,q)=1 is essential. If a and q share a factor, every term shares it, so the progression contains at most one prime. The theorem asserts infinitude, not a specific first prime or short gap.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The totient construction uses this theorem to choose primes in engineered residue classes, making selected matrix entries nonzero while other entries gain prescribed factors. It is distinct from Dirichlet convolution and from other results bearing Dirichlet’s name.

public_glossary.label: discrete mathematics

public_glossary.short_definition: Discrete mathematics studies objects with separate elements, such as integers, graphs, and finite arrangements.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Discrete mathematics studies objects with separate elements, such as integers, graphs, and finite arrangements.
public_glossary.card_definition: Its questions include counting configurations, finding paths in networks, and proving properties of integer sequences. The objects may be finite or infinite; “discrete” does not mean “finite”.

public_glossary.label: discriminant
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Polynomial and number-field discriminants are related but distinct. The discriminant of an order or chosen basis can differ from the field discriminant.
public_glossary.short_definition: A discriminant detects repeated roots or arithmetic degeneracy: a polynomial’s discriminant vanishes exactly when it has a repeated root, while a number field’s discriminant records how its integral arithmetic behaves modulo primes.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A discriminant detects repeated roots or arithmetic degeneracy: a polynomial’s discriminant vanishes exactly when it has a repeated root, while a number field’s discriminant records how its integral arithmetic behaves modulo primes.
public_glossary.card_definition: For a quadratic ax²+bx+c with a≠0, the discriminant is b²−4ac. For a number field, it is the determinant of the trace-pairing matrix of an integral basis. A rational prime ramifies in the number field exactly when it divides the field discriminant.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Polynomial and number-field discriminants are related but are not identical objects. Their values depend on conventions and, for an order or basis discriminant, on the chosen integral data. Always identify which discriminant is meant.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For a degree-n polynomial with leading coefficient a and roots r₁,…,rₙ, its discriminant is a^(2n−2) times the product of (rᵢ−rⱼ)² over i<j. A basis or order discriminant need not equal the field discriminant; an index factor can introduce additional prime divisors. The cited argument excludes the relevant discriminant primes to ensure the reduction and Frobenius steps meet their hypotheses.
public_glossary.scope_note: Polynomial and number-field discriminants are related but are not identical objects. Their values depend on conventions and, for an order or basis discriminant, on the chosen integral data. Always identify which discriminant is meant.
public_glossary.example: For ax²+bx+c, the discriminant is b²−4ac.

public_glossary.label: distance
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Metric geometry. A manuscript may specify a non-Euclidean metric.
public_glossary.short_definition: A distance assigns zero to identical points, positive values to distinct points, and obeys symmetry and the triangle inequality.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A distance assigns zero to identical points, positive values to distinct points, and obeys symmetry and the triangle inequality.
public_glossary.card_definition: On the real line, the distance from x to y is |x-y|; in the complex plane the same formula gives Euclidean distance. A valid distance is nonnegative, symmetric, and zero exactly when its two points coincide.

public_glossary.label: divisibility
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Divisibility is the relation in which one integer is an exact integer multiple of another.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Divisibility is the relation in which one integer is an exact integer multiple of another.

public_glossary.short_definition: An integer d is a divisor of an integer n when n = d·k for some integer k.

public_glossary.card_definition: It includes principles, defined concepts, mechanisms, and guidance connected to source material. These records let agents recover the reasons behind an implementation rather than infer them from code alone.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A doctrine statement expresses a rule or interpretation; implementation evidence shows whether it is enacted.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Keeping the two connected makes disagreements visible. A rule can be clear while its software support is incomplete, or code can change while the explanation remains outdated.
public_glossary.scope_note: Doctrine covers the explicit-meaning layer of the system and is encountered on the Doctrine page and its individual cards, with cross-references reaching into components, paper modules, and the standards they enforce.
public_glossary.example: The axiom "Derivation before assertion", which holds that a claim should be derived from evidence before it is stated as fact, is one doctrine card: a single named principle in the doctrine layer with its own entry on the Doctrine page.

public_glossary.label: Document Object Model
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The DOM represents documents through nodes and operations on them. It can be implemented outside browsers and is distinct from an arbitrary tree-shaped data object.
public_glossary.short_definition: The Document Object Model, or DOM, represents a document as a tree of objects and provides an interface for reading and changing it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The Document Object Model, or DOM, represents a document as a tree of objects and provides an interface for reading and changing it.
public_glossary.card_definition: In a browser, DOM nodes represent a document’s elements and text, with attributes describing the elements. JavaScript can inspect or change this structure. The DOM interface can also be implemented outside browsers; it is distinct from the HTML text stored in a source file.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A DOM change affects the current loaded document; it does not necessarily alter the HTML source file or server copy.
public_glossary.deep_definition: When a browser parses HTML, it creates nodes linked by parent, child, and sibling relationships. Scripts use standard DOM methods to find nodes, attach event listeners, change attributes, and insert controls. Plectis glossary code adds preview controls through this interface while preserving mathematical child nodes. The DOM may differ from downloaded source after scripts run or the browser repairs malformed markup.
public_glossary.scope_note: A DOM change affects the current loaded document; it does not necessarily alter the HTML source file or server copy.
public_glossary.example: A script sets `aria-describedby` on the focused term element in the DOM.

public_glossary.label: dyadic
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Dyadic means related to powers of two, often fractions or intervals built from them.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Dyadic means related to powers of two, often fractions or intervals built from them.
public_glossary.card_definition: A dyadic rational has the form m/2ⁿ for integers m and nonnegative n. Examples include 1/2, 3/8, and 5; each has a terminating binary expansion.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The exact object follows the noun: a dyadic interval or partition is not itself a number.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Dyadic scales are useful when repeatedly halving a range or relating binary digits to arithmetic. They provide a common structure for estimates, subdivisions, and expansions in base two.
public_glossary.scope_note: A dyadic result covers base two unless it says otherwise.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #251 concerns a dyadic series built from prime gaps.

public_glossary.label: dyadic section
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A dyadic section selects an entire subsequence at one residue class modulo a power of two, rather than a finite block of terms.
public_glossary.short_definition: A dyadic section of a sequence a(n) is a subsequence a(2ᵉn+r) obtained by fixing the index modulo a power of two.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A dyadic section of a sequence a(n) is a subsequence a(2ᵉn+r) obtained by fixing the index modulo a power of two.
public_glossary.card_definition: At level one, the two sections are the even and odd terms. At level two, there are four sections indexed by residues 0,1,2,3 modulo 4.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The level e and residue r are part of the section, with 0≤r<2ᵉ. A section is a subsequence, not a finite block. All dyadic sections together form the 2-kernel.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The paper studies ranks of the totient sequence’s sections through each finite level and then the full dyadic kernel.
public_glossary.scope_note: The level e and residue r are part of the section, with 0≤r<2ᵉ. A section is a subsequence, not a finite block. All dyadic sections together form the 2-kernel.
public_glossary.example: At level one, the two sections are the even and odd terms.

public_glossary.label: empirical distribution
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Probability and asymptotic statistics. Evidence from data, not necessarily a theoretical probability law.
public_glossary.short_definition: An empirical distribution puts equal weight on each observation in a finite sample, adding weights when values repeat.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An empirical distribution puts equal weight on each observation in a finite sample, adding weights when values repeat.
public_glossary.card_definition: For observations 1,1,3, the empirical distribution places probability 2/3 on 1 and 1/3 on 3. Each observation receives equal weight before repeated values are combined, so the distribution summarizes observed frequencies.
public_glossary.reader_rule: An empirical distribution comes from a finite sample. A limiting empirical distribution says these frequencies converge as sample size grows; it does not imply that observations are independent, random, or generated by that limiting law.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The prime-gap countermodels preserve the empirical behavior detected by bounded short-block tests while altering the arithmetic conclusion of interest. This shows why matching many statistics can still fail to preserve denominator or irrationality structure.
public_glossary.scope_note: An empirical distribution comes from a finite sample. A limiting empirical distribution says these frequencies converge as sample size grows; it does not imply that observations are independent, random, or generated by that limiting law.

public_glossary.reader_preview: Endogenous means originating within the system or process being discussed.

public_glossary.deep_definition: In the site's research discussion, the concern is self-confirmation: repeated agreement among connected internal checks may provide less independent support than the number of agreeing outputs suggests.

public_glossary.reader_preview: An endpoint is a defined end of a connection, process, path, or investigation; its exact meaning depends on context.

public_glossary.label: environment
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An environment is the surrounding technical, physical, and procedural conditions under which work runs or an observation is made.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An environment is the surrounding technical, physical, and procedural conditions under which work runs or an observation is made.
public_glossary.card_definition: In computing, an environment includes software, hardware, configuration, permissions, files, and services. In experimental work it also includes apparatus, physical conditions, sampling setting, and procedure. These surrounding conditions can change results even when the central instructions or source remain the same.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A result should identify the environmental conditions capable of affecting it, at the level of detail needed for reproduction or comparison.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Environment means the surrounding conditions under which an activity occurs, not only software configuration. For computation it can include operating system, hardware, runtime, libraries, variables, locale, clock, network, permissions, files, and external services. For experiments it also includes apparatus, physical conditions, sampling setting, and procedural controls. Build and runtime environments may differ. When results change, hidden environmental differences are plausible inputs rather than mere noise. Reproducibility requires recording the conditions capable of affecting the outcome at the precision relevant to the claim.
public_glossary.scope_note: The technical, physical, and procedural conditions relevant to an execution or observation.
public_glossary.example: A cold-clone check records the operating system and Lean toolchain used to build the public proof corpus.
public_glossary.non_example: The central source code or experimental instruction alone need not describe every surrounding condition that affects the outcome.

public_glossary.reader_preview: The epistemic control plane is a proposed system layer that uses evidence and uncertainty to govern which actions may proceed.
public_glossary.card_definition: “Epistemic” concerns what is known and how it is justified. The design connects a claim's evidence status to permitted actions, review requirements, and conditions that should stop a change.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The phrase names a design target associated with the Workingness Instrument; the relevant implementation evidence must be checked separately.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Its central idea is that changed evidence should change decisions. Recording uncertainty is useful only when the actions that depend on it respond appropriately.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the runtime layer that would govern action by belief status across the system; a reader meets it in architecture and runtime descriptions and as the forward-looking name for the Workingness Instrument.

public_glossary.label: equality
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An equality states that two expressions represent the same value or mathematical object.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An equality states that two expressions represent the same value or mathematical object.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, 1/2 = 2/4 compares different expressions for the same number. Equality depends on the setting: two functions are equal when they agree as functions, not merely at a few tested inputs.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Distinguish equality from an approximation or a one-way implication.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In Lean, equality is itself a proposition that can require a proof. Two expressions that simplify to the same form may be equal for a more direct reason than expressions requiring a substantial theorem.
public_glossary.scope_note: An equality covers the two expressions, domain, and assumptions stated around it.
public_glossary.example: The equality 12 = 3 × 4 witnesses that 3 divides 12.
public_glossary.non_example: Two decimal approximations that look alike are not necessarily exactly equal.

public_glossary.label: equation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal.
public_glossary.card_definition: It can specify a relation, define a quantity, or ask which values make the equality true. For example, x² = 4 has solutions x = 2 and x = −2 over the real numbers.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The permitted domain and assumptions determine what counts as a solution.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Some equations are identities that hold for every allowed value; others hold only for particular values. A displayed equality in a proof may express a justified transformation rather than a problem to solve.
public_glossary.scope_note: An equation covers the expressions, unknowns, domain, and constraints stated in its formulation.
public_glossary.example: In a denominator argument, an equation obtained by assuming a series rational converts an infinite sum into an exact relation among integers.
public_glossary.non_example: An inequality such as x < 3 compares ordered values; it does not assert equality and is not an equation.

public_glossary.label: equidistribution
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Equidistribution concerns limiting frequencies. A dense sequence need not spend the right proportion of its terms in each interval.
public_glossary.short_definition: A sequence is equidistributed in a region when the long-run proportion of its terms in each suitable subregion equals that subregion’s relative size.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A sequence is equidistributed in a region when the long-run proportion of its terms in each suitable subregion equals that subregion’s relative size.
public_glossary.card_definition: Modulo one, equidistribution means that the proportion of fractional parts in every interval [a,b) tends to b−a as more terms are counted. An interval covering one tenth of [0,1) therefore receives a proportion approaching one tenth; a finite sample need not divide exactly that way.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Equidistribution is a limiting frequency statement over all test intervals or an equivalent test class. Density alone, visual scatter, or visiting every interval does not establish it; correlations can remain even when single-term frequencies are uniform.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The cited passage describes the profile that an orbit under repeated doubling would have if an equidistribution argument succeeded. Elsewhere the manuscript warns that the needed theorem is delicate. The term therefore names a precise limiting-frequency property; its appearance in a proposed route does not assert that the property has been proved for the sequence at hand.
public_glossary.scope_note: Equidistribution is a limiting frequency statement over all test intervals or an equivalent test class. Density alone, visual scatter, or visiting every interval does not establish it; correlations can remain even when single-term frequencies are uniform.
public_glossary.example: The standard modulo-one example asks whether fractional parts visit every interval [a,b) with limiting frequency b-a.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

source_refs.gloss: profile a doubling-orbit equidistribution argument would produce.

public_glossary.label: equivalence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Equivalence means that each of the two named statements implies the other under the same stated domain and hypotheses. It does not follow from similarity, shared examples, or a one-way implication.
public_glossary.short_definition: Two statements are logically equivalent when each implies the other under the same assumptions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Two statements are logically equivalent when each implies the other under the same assumptions.
public_glossary.card_definition: To establish P ↔ Q, one proves both P → Q and Q → P. Either statement can then replace the other within that setting, although one may be easier to understand or use.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A single implication gives a reduction in one direction, not an equivalence.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The papers use equivalences to compare reformulations of open problems. An equivalent reformulation preserves the unresolved question; proving the equivalence alone does not establish either side unconditionally.
public_glossary.scope_note: An equivalence covers the two named statements under their common hypotheses and domain.
public_glossary.example: An irrationality question may be equivalent to the impossibility of an eventually periodic digit pattern.
public_glossary.non_example: Similarity, shared examples, or a one-way implication does not establish equivalence.

public_glossary.label: Paul Erdős
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: This registry only explains how the external term appears here. The external owner, specification, or primary source controls when exact meaning matters.
public_glossary.short_definition: Paul Erdős was a mathematician known for work in number theory, combinatorics, probability, and related fields.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Paul Erdős was a mathematician known for work in number theory, combinatorics, probability, and related fields.
public_glossary.card_definition: He posed and collected many problems, often through extensive collaboration. The site studies selected questions identified by their numbers in the independently maintained Erdős Problems database.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A database number identifies the question; it does not describe its current solution status.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Read the linked problem statement and references for the intended formulation. A paper may establish a related theorem, special case, or obstruction while the numbered question remains open.
public_glossary.scope_note: This entry covers the person and the meaning of his name in the numbered problem labels used on this site.
public_glossary.example: “Erdős #257” means problem 257 in the cited Erdős Problems catalogue.
public_glossary.non_example: Erdős is not the author of this site, and the catalogue number is not a theorem number or difficulty ranking.

public_glossary.label: Erdős problem
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The number identifies an entry in an independently maintained database. It is not a ranking, and the database's status label is its maintainer's current assessment.
public_glossary.short_definition: An Erdős problem is a mathematical question associated with Paul Erdős; this site uses the numbering of the Erdős Problems database.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An Erdős problem is a mathematical question associated with Paul Erdős; this site uses the numbering of the Erdős Problems database.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, “Erdős #249” identifies a particular database entry rather than the 249th theorem in this repository. The entry supplies the question and references needed to understand its origin and context.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Compare a paper's exact statement with the original question before interpreting a result as a solution.
public_glossary.deep_definition: An equivalent reformulation, a finite computation, and an unconditional proof are different forms of progress and should retain their own descriptions.
public_glossary.scope_note: Covers the numbered problem labels and the database they point to; it does not cover Erdős's wider biography, which has its own entry.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #257 asks whether the sum of 1/(2^n − 1) over any infinite set of exponents n is irrational.
public_glossary.non_example: A theorem about one special case of an Erdős problem does not settle the problem, and this site says so wherever it states one.

public_glossary.label: euler product
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Analytic number theory. Named after Euler; unrelated to Euler's modular theorem except historically.
public_glossary.short_definition: An Euler product expresses a quantity as a product of factors associated with individual primes.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An Euler product expresses a quantity as a product of factors associated with individual primes.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, the sum of 1/n² over positive integers equals the product of (1−1/p²)⁻¹ over primes p. Unique prime factorisation explains the correspondence: expanding the factors selects each integer exactly once.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Infinite products and rearrangements require convergence justifications; a finite product over the prime divisors of one integer has a different scope.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The totient formula φ(n) = n∏_{p∣n}(1−1/p) is a finite example. The papers use these separate prime contributions to analyse divisibility and the dependence of totient values on residue classes.
public_glossary.scope_note: Infinite products and rearrangements require convergence justifications; a finite product over the prime divisors of one integer has a different scope.

public_glossary.label: Euler's theorem (modular arithmetic)
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Euler's theorem says that if a is coprime to a positive integer n, then a raised to φ(n) is congruent to 1 modulo n.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Euler's theorem says that if a is coprime to a positive integer n, then a raised to φ(n) is congruent to 1 modulo n.
public_glossary.card_definition: The totient φ(n) counts integers from 1 through n that are coprime to n. For example, φ(10) = 4 and 3⁴ = 81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 10.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The coprimality hypothesis is essential.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The exponent φ(n) gives a period but need not be the smallest one. The papers use such exponents to arrange modular repetition while separately proving any claim about the exact multiplicative order.

public_glossary.reader_preview: An evaluator is a tool or procedure that assesses something against chosen criteria.
public_glossary.card_definition: In Plectis's component model, an evaluator observes inputs and reports its assessment without changing the material being assessed. A separate action is responsible for any repair or update.

public_glossary.label: event listener
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A listener receives dispatched events through a registration mechanism. In a browser it can be a function or an object with a handleEvent method.
public_glossary.short_definition: An event listener is code registered to receive notification when a specified event occurs.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An event listener is code registered to receive notification when a specified event occurs.
public_glossary.card_definition: In the browser, a listener is usually a callback function, though an object with a `handleEvent` method can also serve as one. Events include clicks, key presses, and focus changes. The listener receives information about the event and can respond to it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check the event target, propagation phase, repeat behaviour, and cleanup rules when reasoning about a listener.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Registering a listener lets other code invoke it when an event is dispatched, instead of repeatedly checking for a change. Some browser events travel through capture and bubble phases, allowing a parent element to handle events from its children. Plectis uses this delegation for glossary terms across a page, sharing the interaction code rather than installing a separate set of handlers on every word.
public_glossary.scope_note: Check the event target, propagation phase, repeat behaviour, and cleanup rules when reasoning about a listener.
public_glossary.example: A keydown listener dismisses the open definition card when the reader presses Escape.
public_glossary.non_example: A function that runs once during page parsing without any event registration is not an event listener.

public_glossary.label: eventual property
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An eventual property holds at every index after some finite threshold.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An eventual property holds at every index after some finite threshold.
public_glossary.card_definition: For a sequence indexed by natural numbers, “eventually P(n)” means that there is an N such that P(n) holds for all n ≥ N. Any failures must occur before that threshold.
public_glossary.reader_rule: This is stronger than holding infinitely often or at arbitrarily large indices.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For example, being positive holds eventually for n − 10, whereas being even never holds eventually for all integers n. The papers use this distinction when comparing recurring obstructions with consequences of rationality.
public_glossary.scope_note: This is stronger than holding infinitely often or at arbitrarily large indices.

public_glossary.label: evidence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Evidence is information that supports or challenges a particular claim.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Evidence is information that supports or challenges a particular claim.
public_glossary.card_definition: It may come from a source, observation, proof, calculation, or recorded test. Plectis links claims to their evidence so readers can examine the basis and decide whether it supports the wording used.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Evidence should be interpreted within the conditions under which it was obtained.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A test result, for instance, concerns the version, inputs, and environment tested. A proof has a different scope, determined by its precise statement and assumptions.
public_glossary.scope_note: Evidence covers only the claim, cases, source version, and conditions named by its producing record.
public_glossary.example: A result record from a local check is evidence that the declared fixtures passed at the recorded commit.
public_glossary.non_example: A confident summary or repeated assertion is not evidence merely because it sounds precise.

public_glossary.label: evidence band
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The bands describe the kind of support a statement has in this project's records. They are not a grading of importance.
public_glossary.short_definition: An evidence band labels the kind of support attached to a statement in a mathematical working record.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An evidence band labels the kind of support attached to a statement in a mathematical working record.
public_glossary.card_definition: The records use labels such as Lean for formal checking, Cert for a checked certificate, Math for mathematical argument, Cited for a referenced result, and Open for an unresolved obligation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: These labels describe different sources of support, not interchangeable levels of approval.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A separate scope description indicates whether the statement covers listed cases, a bounded range, arbitrarily large parameters, or all allowed parameters. Both the evidence and its reach matter.
public_glossary.scope_note: Covers the tags used in the two long working records and mirrored on the problem pages.
public_glossary.example: A lemma tagged Cert was verified by exact arithmetic for the listed values only.
public_glossary.non_example: A Math-band statement is not machine-checked, even when a Lean lemma nearby looks similar.

public_glossary.label: exact rational arithmetic
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Exact rational arithmetic calculates with integer numerators and denominators instead of rounded decimal values.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Exact rational arithmetic calculates with integer numerators and denominators instead of rounded decimal values.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, 1/3 + 1/6 is stored and simplified to 1/2 using integer operations. Provided the implementation supports the required integer sizes, these operations introduce no rounding error.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Exact calculation still depends on correct inputs, algorithms, and interpretation.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The papers use it when a tiny difference or precise equality matters. It settles the computed rational expression, while an argument about an infinite limit may also need a proved bound on the omitted terms.
public_glossary.scope_note: Applies to computations over the rationals; irrational quantities are not represented exactly this way.
public_glossary.example: One third plus one sixth is stored as one half, not as 0.5000000001.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: executable cross-section
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Executable cross-section is a local ai_workflow/Plectis construct for the published runnable selection. No generally accepted external category, whole-system coverage, or equivalence with an unpublished system is claimed.
public_glossary.short_definition: An executable cross-section is a selected part of a larger system that can be run and inspected on its own.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An executable cross-section is a selected part of a larger system that can be run and inspected on its own.
public_glossary.card_definition: Plectis publishes components with the source, inputs, checks, and records needed to examine their behaviour. The selection aims to make a working mechanism available without requiring the entire private environment.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Its scope is the included material and the dependencies declared for it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A successful run provides evidence about that public selection. Claims about the larger system need their own support, especially where unpublished components or interactions are involved.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the published runnable selection and its recorded checks. It excludes unpublished components, private data, and claims about whole-system behaviour.
public_glossary.example: Plectis is an executable cross-section because its public components can be cloned, run locally, and inspected through their result records.
public_glossary.non_example: A video of a private application is not an executable cross-section because the viewer cannot run or inspect the demonstrated mechanism.

public_glossary.label: execution
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Execution is the running of instructions or the actual performance of a planned operation.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Execution is the running of instructions or the actual performance of a planned operation.
public_glossary.card_definition: Source code, a command, or a workflow description records intended work; execution is the event in which a computer or actor carries it out with particular inputs and conditions.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A plan or runnable artifact does not establish that execution began, reached its final step, or produced the intended result.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Execution occurs in a concrete environment and can differ from the plan because of inputs, configuration, permissions, dependencies, timing, or failure. It may finish successfully, stop partway, remain active, or complete with unwanted side effects. Logs and receipts can show which instructions ran, while outputs and state checks show what changed. A successful process exit establishes only the success condition defined by that process; it does not automatically prove semantic correctness, publication, deployment, or acceptance by another system.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers command, program, workflow, test, and proof-checking runs.
public_glossary.example: Executing the builder reads source data and writes generated public files.
public_glossary.non_example: Displaying a command in a code block does not execute it.

public_glossary.label: existential quantifier
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The mathematical sense stated here; related software or ordinary-language uses are distinguished where relevant.
public_glossary.short_definition: An existential quantifier states that at least one element of a specified domain satisfies a property.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An existential quantifier states that at least one element of a specified domain satisfies a property.
public_glossary.card_definition: The symbol ∃ means “there exists.” To establish ∃n ∈ ℕ, n² = 4, the number 2 is a witness. “At least one” does not mean exactly one: a separate uniqueness claim is needed to exclude other witnesses.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A witness must satisfy every required condition; changing the domain can change whether a witness exists.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In ∀x ∃y, the choice of y may depend on x. In ∃y ∀x, one y must work for all x. Lean statements preserve this distinction, which can make a conditional or uniform claim substantially stronger.
public_glossary.scope_note: A witness must satisfy every required condition; changing the domain can change whether a witness exists.
public_glossary.example: Representative source: governed vocabulary term_registry.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: exit code
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An exit code is the small numeric status a process returns when it finishes.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An exit code is the small numeric status a process returns when it finishes.
public_glossary.card_definition: By convention zero usually reports success and nonzero values distinguish kinds of failure, though each program defines its own meanings. Scripts and workflow engines use the code to decide whether to continue, retry, or stop. Output text and exit status are separate evidence.
public_glossary.reader_rule: An exit code must be interpreted using the producing command’s contract; nonzero does not always mean the same failure, and zero does not validate claims beyond that command.
public_glossary.deep_definition: An exit code is a process-level completion signal, usually an integer made available to the parent shell or orchestrator. Unix convention reserves zero for success and nonzero values for exceptional outcomes, but individual programs define the detailed mapping. Standard output and error text may explain the result yet remain separate from this status. Signals, crashes, wrappers, pipelines, and timeouts can transform what callers observe. Reliable automation therefore interprets codes through the command’s documented contract and preserves enough output to diagnose which condition actually occurred.
public_glossary.scope_note: An exit code reports one process completion status under that command’s documented convention; wrappers, signals, and orchestrators may map outcomes differently.
public_glossary.example: A tool documents exit 0 as success, exit 1 as a detected difference, and exit 2 as invalid invocation, allowing its caller to respond differently.
public_glossary.non_example: A nonzero code is not universally the same failure, and exit 0 does not establish claims beyond the command’s stated check.

public_glossary.label: exogenous
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Exogenous means originating outside the system or process under discussion.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Exogenous means originating outside the system or process under discussion.
public_glossary.card_definition: An external observation, event, or judgement can be exogenous relative to the process being studied. The classification depends on the chosen boundary: a signal can be external to one component but internal to the organisation containing it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Outside origin does not by itself guarantee accuracy or independence.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Plectis uses the term when discussing evidence and criticism that do not arise solely from the workflow producing the work. The source's expertise and dependencies still need assessment.
public_glossary.scope_note: Describes the source of a process or judgement. It does not mean true.
public_glossary.example: An expert saying the main lemma is a known result would be an exogenous report.
public_glossary.non_example: A green Lean run on the author's machine is not an exogenous judgement of importance.

public_glossary.label: exogenous truth
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Exogenous and endogenous keep their ordinary meanings: from outside and from inside a system. This compound names a judgement whose source is outside the process being judged. No technical claim about economics or biology is intended.
public_glossary.short_definition: “Exogenous truth” is this project's phrase for judgement brought in from outside the process being judged.
public_glossary.reader_preview: “Exogenous truth” is this project's phrase for judgement brought in from outside the process being judged.
public_glossary.card_definition: It refers to an independent reader examining the public evidence and forming their own assessment, including disagreement with the project's account. The phrase stresses an external source of criticism or correction.
public_glossary.reader_rule: It does not mean that an outsider's judgement is automatically true.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The value lies in different evidence, expertise, or assumptions entering the discussion. A claim still needs to be assessed on its merits, whether it comes from inside or outside the project.
public_glossary.scope_note: Describes the source of a judgement about the project. It does not claim that every outside reaction is correct.
public_glossary.example: An expert reading one problem page and saying the main lemma is a known result would be exogenous truth, and would be welcome.
public_glossary.non_example: A model, prompted by the author, declaring the work important is still endogenous.

public_glossary.label: exponent
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An exponent specifies a power: in bⁿ, b is the base and n is the exponent.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An exponent specifies a power: in bⁿ, b is the base and n is the exponent.
public_glossary.card_definition: For a positive integer n, bⁿ means multiplying n copies of b. With nonzero b, b⁰ = 1 and b⁻ⁿ = 1/bⁿ. Fractional and real exponents require further definitions and domain conditions.
public_glossary.reader_rule: In digit expansions and arithmetic series, check whether the exponent is restricted to integers.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The expression 2ⁿ − 1 subtracts one after taking the power. It differs from 2ⁿ⁻¹, which lowers the exponent before calculating the power.
public_glossary.scope_note: Exponent covers the power index in the named expression, sequence, or support.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #257 sums `1/(2^n-1)` over an infinite set of positive exponents `n`.
public_glossary.non_example: The exponent `n` is not the same number as the power `2^n`.

public_glossary.label: exponential backoff
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A retry schedule whose delay grows multiplicatively after successive failures, usually subject to a maximum; constant immediate retries are outside this sense.
public_glossary.short_definition: Exponential backoff is a retry schedule that increases the delay after each consecutive failure, usually by multiplying it by a fixed factor.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Exponential backoff is a retry schedule that increases the delay after each consecutive failure, usually by multiplying it by a fixed factor.
public_glossary.card_definition: Growing delays reduce pressure on an unavailable or rate-limited service and give it time to recover. Practical schedules normally set maximum delays, attempt limits, and an overall deadline.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Retry only failures that may recover, respect server guidance, and stop within a stated attempt or time budget.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A common schedule waits roughly one unit, then two, four, and eight, capped at a maximum. Successful work resets the failure count. Exponential backoff controls retry timing; it does not make a non-idempotent operation safe to repeat or fix invalid input. Plectis provider-routing prose discusses backing off across services after rate limits, where bounded delays prevent a tight failure loop.
public_glossary.scope_note: Retry only failures that may recover, respect server guidance, and stop within a stated attempt or time budget.
public_glossary.example: A client waits 1, 2, 4, then at most 8 seconds between retryable requests.
public_glossary.non_example: Immediately retrying forever at a constant rate is not exponential backoff.

public_glossary.label: exponential growth
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Asymptotic growth. Not every rapidly growing function is exponential in the strict sense.
public_glossary.short_definition: Exact exponential growth multiplies a positive quantity by the same factor greater than one at each step.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Exact exponential growth multiplies a positive quantity by the same factor greater than one at each step.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, 2ⁿ doubles with each unit increase of n and eventually exceeds every fixed power nᵏ. Papers also use exponential upper or lower bounds, such as aₙ ≤ C·2ⁿ; such a bound does not say aₙ itself doubles each step.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The base, input variable, and direction of the bound matter; exponential growth is not a synonym for any rapid growth.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Moduli and carry barriers in the Mersenne-support work operate on exponential scales, making polynomial savings insufficient.
public_glossary.scope_note: The base, input variable, and direction of the bound matter; exponential growth is not a synonym for any rapid growth.

public_glossary.label: exponential sum
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: An exponential sum has a specified range, coefficients, and phase. Its name alone gives no cancellation estimate.
public_glossary.short_definition: An exponential sum is a finite sum of complex phases, commonly Σ a_n exp(2πi f(n)), used to measure cancellation or arithmetic regularity.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An exponential sum is a finite sum of complex phases, commonly Σ a_n exp(2πi f(n)), used to measure cancellation or arithmetic regularity.
public_glossary.card_definition: Each complex phase can be pictured as an arrow. Arrows pointing in different directions may nearly cancel, while aligned arrows reinforce one another. For n>1, all nth roots of unity sum to zero. Bounds on such cancellation are useful in number theory.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The coefficients, range, and phase function are part of the definition in each use. Calling an expression an exponential sum does not by itself supply a bound. It is distinct from an infinite exponential series.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The paper proposes a weighted exponential sum of totient differences as a diagnostic for a binary word. A strong uniform bound could support distribution claims, while isolated numerical cancellation would not establish them.
public_glossary.scope_note: The coefficients, range, and phase function are part of the definition in each use. Calling an expression an exponential sum does not by itself supply a bound. It is distinct from an infinite exponential series.
public_glossary.example: If phases point in many directions, their vector sum can be much smaller than the sum of their lengths.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: exposition
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The staged meaning used here is Terence Tao's, from Mathematics in the age of AI (arXiv:2608.16753). This site does not own or redefine that stage; community acceptance remains external.
public_glossary.short_definition: Mathematical exposition explains a result, its proof, and why the argument works for its intended readers.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Mathematical exposition explains a result, its proof, and why the argument works for its intended readers.
public_glossary.card_definition: Good exposition states the assumptions, introduces notation, identifies the main idea, and distinguishes new work from earlier results. It makes a proof easier to assess and use without weakening its precise claim.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Clear writing supports verification but cannot replace missing mathematical reasoning.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The site treats exposition as a separate task from obtaining a checked proof. A formal declaration may be valid while still needing an explanation that lets another mathematician understand or continue the work.
public_glossary.scope_note: The word is Tao's. The local use is: write the human-readable account that would let someone else give the talk. The local use is not: declare the talk given.
public_glossary.example: A long reasoning-surface PDF that keeps the failed routes beside the checked lemmas is an attempt at exposition of a still-open problem.
public_glossary.non_example: A kernel-accepted proof with no account of the hard step is verification without exposition.

public_glossary.label: factor
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A factor is one of the quantities multiplied together to make a product.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A factor is one of the quantities multiplied together to make a product.
public_glossary.card_definition: In 12 = 3·4, both 3 and 4 are factors of 12. For integers, saying that d is a factor of n usually means that d divides n exactly.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Factorisation expresses an object as a product of its factors.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In algebra, factors may be expressions: x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1). The setting determines which factors count as irreducible and what uniqueness of factorisation means. Factoring can expose roots or divisibility conditions that are hidden in the expanded expression.
public_glossary.scope_note: Factor covers the product and algebraic domain named in context.
public_glossary.example: 3 and 4 are factors in the product 3 × 4 = 12.
public_glossary.non_example: A summand in 3 + 4 is not a factor because the operation is addition.

public_glossary.label: factorial
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The factorial of a nonnegative integer n is the product of the integers from 1 through n, with the value at zero defined as 1.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The factorial of a nonnegative integer n is the product of the integers from 1 through n, with the value at zero defined as 1.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, 4! = 24. Factorials count arrangements of n distinct objects and also provide rapidly growing, highly divisible denominators in number-theory problems.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The exclamation mark here is mathematical notation, not punctuation indicating emphasis.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Expressions such as n! − 1 and (n − 1)! have very different values and divisibility properties. The paper's parentheses and order of operations are therefore part of the statement being studied.
public_glossary.scope_note: The usual whole-number factorial, not the gamma function unless a page says so.
public_glossary.non_example: Calling a proof 'factorial' in the everyday sense of 'having many factors' is not this term.

public_glossary.label: factorisation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Factorisation writes a number or algebraic expression as a product of simpler factors.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Factorisation writes a number or algebraic expression as a product of simpler factors.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, 60 = 2²·3·5 is the prime factorisation of 60. Every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation, apart from the order in which its factors are written.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Uniqueness depends on the mathematical setting when the objects are more general than integers.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The papers use factorisation to study divisibility, common factors, and the denominators of sums. A convenient factorisation can reveal constraints that are hard to see from a decimal value.
public_glossary.scope_note: Factorisation covers the named integer, polynomial, or algebraic expression and the permitted factor class.
public_glossary.example: Euler's totient can be computed from the prime factorisation of its input.
public_glossary.non_example: Writing a number as `1 × n` is formally a product but not the nontrivial factorisation usually sought.

public_glossary.label: fail-closed
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Fail-closed means a composite is only as trusted as its weakest required part, and missing evidence blocks rather than silently passes.
public_glossary.short_definition: Fail-closed means withholding an action when a required condition cannot be established.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Fail-closed means withholding an action when a required condition cannot be established.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, a publication gate may stop when a required check is missing or its result cannot be read. Plectis uses this behaviour where proceeding without evidence would wrongly treat uncertainty as permission.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The required conditions and the action being withheld must be explicit.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Failing closed can prevent an unsupported action, but it does not prove the underlying artifact is faulty. The next step may be to obtain the missing evidence or repair the check.
public_glossary.scope_note: Doctrine AX-5 copy.
public_glossary.example: AX-5: missing evidence defaults to blocked rather than silently passing.

public_glossary.non_example: Fail-closed is not a claim that the public site is a safety-certified product.

public_glossary.label: failure class propagation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Failure-class propagation tests whether one local break recurs across sibling surfaces before widening the repair; it is not permission to apply one fix everywhere.
public_glossary.short_definition: Failure-class propagation checks whether a discovered fault also affects other cases for the same reason.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Failure-class propagation checks whether a discovered fault also affects other cases for the same reason.
public_glossary.card_definition: Plectis starts with the local failure, identifies its cause, and inspects related surfaces that share the relevant mechanism. Confirmed instances can then be repaired together through the common source or rule.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Similarity alone is not enough to assume that another case has the same fault.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The aim is to fix a recurring cause without expanding the repair to unrelated work. A useful record states which cases were examined and where the explanation stops applying.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers how the system turns a local defect into a bounded, checked repair across related surfaces. A reader meets it in the doctrine and in components such as the Pattern Binding Contract, where a local pattern is bound to its proven extent with a stated boundary rather than patched once or expanded without limit.
public_glossary.example: The Pattern Binding Contract is a concrete instance: it takes an observed pattern, binds it to the sibling surfaces where the same shape genuinely recurs, and fixes the extent of the binding so the repair neither stops at the first case nor spreads past where the pattern holds.

public_glossary.non_example: Failure class propagation is not patching only the one spot that broke, and it is not turning a single bug into an unbounded sweep across the whole system. It is a bounded repair sized to the siblings that were actually checked.

relationships.gloss: Moves a local failure into a bounded reusable class across the lattice.
Annexes can pressure the class hypothesis when the primitive is unsettled.

public_glossary.label: failure modes
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Failure modes are the distinct ways something can fail to meet its intended purpose.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Failure modes are the distinct ways something can fail to meet its intended purpose.
public_glossary.card_definition: A check might accept bad input, reject good input, use stale data, or fail to run. These are different failure modes because their causes, evidence, and repairs can differ.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Name the mechanism of failure, not just the fact that a result is wrong.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Plectis uses negative cases and recorded incidents to make such failures inspectable. Covering known modes improves a check, while new situations may still reveal modes that were not anticipated.
public_glossary.scope_note: Names classes of break. It does not mean every failure is interesting or that the project has catalogued all of them.
public_glossary.example: A proof assistant accepting a statement that is not the original problem is a failure mode of translation, even when the check is green.
public_glossary.non_example: A deliberate refusal of unsafe input is successful protection, not a failure mode of the gate.

public_glossary.label: fallback
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The stated technical meaning; distinct disciplinary senses are identified where the site uses them.
public_glossary.short_definition: A fallback is an alternative behavior used when a preferred route is unavailable, unsuitable, or fails.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A fallback is an alternative behavior used when a preferred route is unavailable, unsuitable, or fails.
public_glossary.card_definition: A service may use cached data when a live provider is down, or switch to a simpler algorithm when resources are limited. The result can remain useful while losing freshness, accuracy, capacity, or assurance.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Fallback behavior is defined by its trigger, alternative source or method, preserved capabilities, reduced guarantees, duration, and route back to normal operation.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Fallbacks improve resilience when their reduced contract is explicit. A silent fallback can instead hide primary failures, make stale results look current, or produce inconsistent behavior across users. The alternative may fail independently or depend on the same underlying resource, so it is not automatically redundant. Systems often record fallback activation, expose degraded status, bound how long cached or approximate results remain acceptable, and test recovery. A fallback is a planned contingency, whereas arbitrary error swallowing merely conceals failure.
public_glossary.scope_note: Fallback behavior is defined by its trigger, alternative source or method, preserved capabilities, reduced guarantees, duration, and route back to normal operation.
