public_glossary.label: riemann map

public_glossary.label: ring
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A ring need not allow division by every nonzero element. The algebra used here takes rings to have a multiplicative identity.
public_glossary.short_definition: A ring is a set with an abelian-group addition and an associative multiplication that distributes over addition.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A ring is a set with an abelian-group addition and an associative multiplication that distributes over addition.
public_glossary.card_definition: Addition has a zero, additive inverses, and the commutative law; multiplication is associative and distributes on both sides. The rings used here have a multiplicative identity 1. A commutative ring additionally has ab=ba. The integers are an example, even though most integers have no multiplicative inverse.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Conventions vary on whether every ring must have a multiplicative identity 1; the surrounding algebra here uses rings with 1. A ring need not be a field, because division by nonzero elements may fail.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Polynomial rings and rings of integers let algebra proceed without assuming division by every nonzero element. Some authors allow rings without an identity, so that convention must be checked. The papers use commutative rings with identity as the setting for coefficients, ideals, and quotients. A field is a commutative ring in which 1≠0 and every nonzero element is invertible.
public_glossary.scope_note: Conventions vary on whether every ring must have a multiplicative identity 1; the surrounding algebra here uses rings with 1. A ring need not be a field, because division by nonzero elements may fail.
public_glossary.example: The integers form a commutative ring: they can be added, subtracted, and multiplied, but most nonzero integers have no multiplicative inverse in the integers.

public_glossary.label: ring automorphism
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: An automorphism is invertible and preserves ring operations. An endomorphism preserves the operations but need not be invertible.
public_glossary.short_definition: A ring automorphism is a bijective map from a ring to itself that preserves addition, multiplication, and the multiplicative identity when rings are unital.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A ring automorphism is a bijective map from a ring to itself that preserves addition, multiplication, and the multiplicative identity when rings are unital.
public_glossary.card_definition: Substituting x↦x+1 in a polynomial ring is an automorphism: substituting x↦x−1 reverses it. The map preserves polynomial sums and products even though individual coefficients change.
public_glossary.reader_rule: It must be both structure-preserving and invertible. A ring endomorphism need not be bijective. The base ring may also be required to remain fixed, in which case one speaks of an automorphism over that base.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The paper uses a coordinate translation x_i↦x_i+e^(i). Calling it an automorphism certifies that the substitution loses no polynomial information and can be undone.
public_glossary.scope_note: It must be both structure-preserving and invertible. A ring endomorphism need not be bijective. The base ring may also be required to remain fixed, in which case one speaks of an automorphism over that base.
public_glossary.example: Substituting x↦x+1 in a polynomial ring is an automorphism: substituting x↦x−1 reverses it.

public_glossary.label: rollback
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A rollback restores an earlier state, but may leave effects already observed outside the system. It does not make a failed change cease to have happened.
public_glossary.short_definition: A rollback returns a system, transaction, or recorded state to an earlier state after a change.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A rollback returns a system, transaction, or recorded state to an earlier state after a change.
public_glossary.card_definition: Rollback may reverse a database transaction, redeploy an earlier release, restore a backup, or apply a compensating change. The available guarantee depends on the system.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Restoring local state does not necessarily undo effects already observed by another person or system.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A rollback plan identifies the prior state, trigger, procedure, authority, and evidence that restoration succeeded. Some operations are fully reversible; others require compensation because messages were sent, data escaped, or outside systems changed. Plectis treats rollback evidence as one part of release authority. A Git revert creates a new inverse commit and differs from moving a branch pointer back.

public_glossary.label: root multiplicity

public_glossary.card_definition: For a nonzero polynomial, a root a has multiplicity k when p(z) = (z − a)ᵏq(z) with q(a) ≠ 0. A simple root has multiplicity one; a multiple root has larger multiplicity.

public_glossary.deep_definition: For example, (z − 1)²(z + 2) has three roots counted with multiplicity but only two distinct roots. public_glossary.label: root of a polynomial
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A polynomial root is a zero of the polynomial, distinct from a root directory or a root node in a hierarchy.
public_glossary.short_definition: A number r for which a polynomial f has value f(r)=0.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A number r for which a polynomial f has value f(r)=0.

public_glossary.label: root of unity
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: An nth root of unity has order dividing n. A primitive nth root has order exactly n.
public_glossary.short_definition: An nth root of unity is a complex number ζ satisfying ζⁿ=1; it is primitive when no smaller positive power of ζ equals one.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An nth root of unity is a complex number ζ satisfying ζⁿ=1; it is primitive when no smaller positive power of ζ equals one.
public_glossary.card_definition: For n=4 the roots are 1, i, −1, and −i. The primitive fourth roots are i and −i, because their exact multiplicative order is four.
public_glossary.reader_rule: “Primitive root of unity” is different from a primitive root modulo an integer. Exact order matters: 1 is an nth root of unity for every n but is primitive only for n=1.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For a fixed positive integer n, the nth roots of unity form a finite cyclic group under multiplication. Its generators are the primitive nth roots and are the roots of the nth cyclotomic polynomial. All nth roots of a nonzero complex number are obtained from one chosen root by multiplying by each nth root of unity. A primitive root modulo an integer is a related but different object: a residue class generating a modular unit group.
public_glossary.scope_note: “Primitive root of unity” is different from a primitive root modulo an integer. Exact order matters: 1 is an nth root of unity for every n but is primitive only for n=1.
public_glossary.example: For n=4 the roots are 1, i, −1, and −i.

public_glossary.label: saddle point
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Calculus, topology, and dynamical systems. The word also appears informally for bottlenecks; the mathematical sense is critical-point structure.
public_glossary.short_definition: A critical point where a function rises in some directions and falls in others.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A critical point where a function rises in some directions and falls in others.
public_glossary.card_definition: For u(x,y)=x²-y², the origin is a saddle point: u increases along the x-axis and decreases along the y-axis. It is critical because the gradient vanishes, but it is neither a local maximum nor minimum.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A nondegenerate planar saddle has one rising and one falling direction in suitable local coordinates. Degenerate or multiple critical points may have more complicated prongs, so conclusions proved for simple saddles do not automatically extend.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Polynomial sublevel components can merge at saddle levels. The associated separatrices and local branches describe how root-containing regions attach, while global path construction still requires controlling what happens outside the local saddle neighbourhood.

public_glossary.label: sandbox
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A sandbox is an environment that enforces specific limits on the files, networks, devices, processes, or privileges available to running code.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A sandbox is an environment that enforces specific limits on the files, networks, devices, processes, or privileges available to running code.
public_glossary.card_definition: Sandboxing reduces the reach of mistakes or hostile behaviour by restricting selected capabilities. Its protection is only as broad as the configured boundaries and the enforcement layer that maintains them.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A sandbox confines effects only across its enforced boundaries; allowed paths, network access, inherited credentials, host interfaces, and escape mechanisms remain inside its effective capability set.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A sandbox runs code with a constrained view of its surroundings. Depending on the design, it may limit filesystem paths, network destinations, system calls, devices, process creation, memory, time, or credentials. These restrictions reduce potential impact, but they do not establish that the code is correct or safe. A sandbox that permits writes to a shared directory still allows damage there, and a network-enabled sandbox can affect reachable services. Isolation also depends on correct configuration and enforcement; a vulnerability in the boundary can permit escape. Sandbox claims therefore describe concrete restrictions rather than absolute protection.
public_glossary.scope_note: A sandbox covers the resources and permissions explicitly constrained for one execution context.
public_glossary.example: A fixture check may run in a temporary directory with no network or access to private repository state.
public_glossary.non_example: Running in a temporary folder alone does not prove that network, process, or credential access is sandboxed.

public_glossary.label: separable extension
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Separable refers to distinct roots of minimal polynomials, not spatial separation. Algebraic extensions in characteristic zero are separable.
public_glossary.short_definition: An algebraic extension L/K is separable when every element of L has a minimal polynomial over K with no repeated roots in a splitting field.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An algebraic extension L/K is separable when every element of L has a minimal polynomial over K with no repeated roots in a splitting field.
public_glossary.card_definition: Every algebraic extension of a field of characteristic zero, including number fields over Q, is separable. In positive characteristic, repeated-root phenomena such as x^p−a can make an extension inseparable.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Separable does not mean that different elements of L are unequal or spatially separated. It is a property of minimal-polynomial roots and is relative to the base field.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Separability supplies distinct embeddings of the extension into an algebraic closure. With normality, those embeddings land back in L and become the elements of its Galois group.

public_glossary.short_definition: A sequence is an indexed family of terms, usually ordered by natural-number positions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A sequence is an indexed family of terms, usually ordered by natural-number positions.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, aₙ = 1/n for n ≥ 1 gives 1, 1/2, 1/3, … . The index identifies each position, and repeated values are allowed.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The starting index and formula or recurrence are part of the definition.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A sequence lists terms; a series adds them. That distinction matters because a sequence tending to zero can still have a divergent sum, as happens with the harmonic sequence and harmonic series.
public_glossary.scope_note: Sequence covers the ordered family and index domain named in the statement.
public_glossary.example: The consecutive primes form an increasing sequence whose successive differences are the prime gaps.
public_glossary.non_example: An unordered set containing the same values is not the same object as the sequence.

public_glossary.label: series
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A mathematical series is a sum of terms from a sequence, often extending over infinitely many indices.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A mathematical series is a sum of terms from a sequence, often extending over infinitely many indices.
public_glossary.card_definition: The expression ∑ aₙ is understood through its finite partial sums. When those partial sums approach a finite limit, the series converges and that limit is its sum.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A time series is a different use: a sequence of observations indexed by time, not necessarily added together.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The papers specify their summation indices and convergence conditions. Omitting the initial index or changing the order can matter, especially when terms are undefined or convergence is not absolute.
public_glossary.scope_note: Covers infinite sums in the formal-mathematics material and ordered data streams in software and forecasting components.
public_glossary.example: A reciprocal Erdős series is an infinite sum; US10Y, CPI, and paired-loss series are ordered data records.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: series tail
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The tail of a series is the part remaining after a chosen finite number of terms.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The tail of a series is the part remaining after a chosen finite number of terms.
public_glossary.card_definition: For ∑ aₙ starting at 1, the tail after N is ∑ over n > N of aₙ. When the series converges, this equals the full sum minus its Nth partial sum.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A convergent series has tails tending to zero, although multiplying them by a growing factor may change that behaviour.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The papers often study scaled tails to expose integer or divisibility conditions. Those arithmetic properties require more than the fact that the unscaled tail becomes small.
public_glossary.scope_note: A convergent series has tails tending to zero, although multiplying them by a growing factor may change that behaviour.

public_glossary.label: server
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A program or system acting in response to requests from clients; a standalone program is not a server merely because it runs on a computer.
public_glossary.short_definition: A server is a program or computer that receives requests and provides data, computation, or another service to clients.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A server is a program or computer that receives requests and provides data, computation, or another service to clients.
public_glossary.card_definition: A server may host web pages, expose an API, store files, run tools, or coordinate jobs. One machine can run several server processes, and one service can span several machines.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Distinguish the server program, its host machine, and the service it provides; they are related but not identical.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Clients and servers describe roles in an interaction rather than permanent kinds of machine. A program can be a client in one exchange and a server in another. Servers must validate requests, enforce authorization, manage capacity, and report failures without exposing secrets. Plectis pages mention tool servers and public static hosting; the public site serves files while tool servers expose callable operations. A server response is evidence of that exchange, not proof of every claim in its payload.
public_glossary.scope_note: Distinguish the server program, its host machine, and the service it provides; they are related but not identical.
public_glossary.example: A web server returns a prebuilt HTML page in response to an HTTPS GET request.
public_glossary.non_example: A standalone script that neither listens for nor receives requests is not acting as a server.

public_glossary.label: set
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A set is a collection determined by which elements belong to it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A set is a collection determined by which elements belong to it.
public_glossary.card_definition: Order and repetition do not change a set: {1, 2} and {2, 1, 1} describe the same set. The notation x ∈ A says that x belongs to A.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A sequence or multiset keeps information that an ordinary set discards.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This distinction matters in the papers when selecting exponents or counting roots. A polynomial's roots as a set ignore repeated occurrences, while roots counted with multiplicity carry additional information.
public_glossary.scope_note: Covers mathematical membership collections used in Plectis statements and certificates, especially exponent and support sets.
public_glossary.example: In S_F(b), F is a finite set of exponents; the corresponding open problem asks about every infinite support set.
public_glossary.non_example: A sequence is not merely a set because order and repetition can matter.

public_glossary.label: set intersection
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The mathematical sense stated here; related software or ordinary-language uses are distinguished where relevant.
public_glossary.short_definition: The intersection of sets contains exactly the elements common to all of them.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The intersection of sets contains exactly the elements common to all of them.
public_glossary.card_definition: For A = {1,2} and B = {2,3}, A ∩ B is {2}. If the sets have no common element, their intersection is empty. Membership in an intersection is an “and” condition: every participating membership requirement must hold.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Two nonempty sets can have an empty intersection, so separate existence statements do not establish a common witness.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The papers use intersections to combine restrictions on candidates, indices, or regions. Producing something that satisfies each condition separately can be much easier than producing one object satisfying all conditions together.
public_glossary.scope_note: Two nonempty sets can have an empty intersection, so separate existence statements do not establish a common witness.

public_glossary.label: set membership
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The mathematical sense stated here; related software or ordinary-language uses are distinguished where relevant.
public_glossary.short_definition: Set membership is the relation saying that an object is one of the elements of a set.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Set membership is the relation saying that an object is one of the elements of a set.
public_glossary.card_definition: The symbol x ∈ A means “x belongs to A”; x ∉ A means it does not. For example, 2 ∈ {1,2,3}, but 5 ∉ {1,2,3}. Membership differs from subset inclusion: an element belongs to a set, whereas a subset contains only elements of that set.
public_glossary.reader_rule: An element can itself be a set, so braces and the declared types matter when reading nested collections.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Statements such as z ∈ U and n ∈ A specify which points or indices are allowed. These restrictions often carry the hypotheses needed for a formula, proof step, or chosen witness to be valid.

public_glossary.label: set union
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The mathematical sense stated here; related software or ordinary-language uses are distinguished where relevant.
public_glossary.short_definition: The union of sets contains every element belonging to at least one of them.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The union of sets contains every element belonging to at least one of them.
public_glossary.card_definition: For A = {1,2} and B = {2,3}, the union A ∪ B is {1,2,3}. The shared element 2 appears once because sets record membership, not repeated occurrences. A union can also combine an infinite family of sets.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Membership in a union is an “or” condition, allowing membership in several of the component sets.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This differs from intersection, which requires simultaneous membership. In the mathematics pages, unions describe combined regions or collections of allowable cases; proving a property of each piece may require further work before it holds for the union.
public_glossary.scope_note: Membership in a union is an “or” condition, allowing membership in several of the component sets.

public_glossary.label: side effect
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: An observable change beyond returning a value, such as writing a file or changing external state; constructing a local value alone is outside this sense.
public_glossary.short_definition: A side effect is an observable change a computation makes beyond returning its direct result.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A side effect is an observable change a computation makes beyond returning its direct result.
public_glossary.card_definition: Side effects include writing files, changing a database, sending a message, starting a process, or modifying shared state. The same function may have both a return value and side effects.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify and authorize side effects separately from calculating or previewing a result.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Writing a file, changing a shared object, sending a request, or displaying output affects something beyond a function’s return value. Repeating such work can repeat the effect, which matters for retries and recovery. Plectis distinguishes isolated fixture calculations from actions on live files, accounts, and services. Reading a clock or random input is also an effect in broader programming terminology because it makes a result depend on outside state, even when the read itself changes nothing observable.
public_glossary.scope_note: Identify and authorize side effects separately from calculating or previewing a result.
public_glossary.example: A command returns success and also writes a generated report to disk.
public_glossary.non_example: Constructing a new value entirely in local memory has no externally observable side effect.

public_glossary.label: simple critical point
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A simple critical point of a complex polynomial p is a simple root of its derivative: p′(c) = 0 and p″(c) ≠ 0.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A simple critical point of a complex polynomial p is a simple root of its derivative: p′(c) = 0 and p″(c) ≠ 0.
public_glossary.card_definition: Near such a point, the first nonconstant term in the polynomial's local expansion is quadratic. This gives a specific local branching structure that differs from a higher-multiplicity critical point.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When p(c) is nonzero, the associated modulus geometry has the ordinary nondegenerate saddle form.
public_glossary.deep_definition: If p(c) = 0, the modulus instead vanishes there, so it should not be described by that same saddle claim. The papers' extra hypotheses distinguish these cases.
public_glossary.scope_note: When p(c) is nonzero, the associated modulus geometry has the ordinary nondegenerate saddle form.

public_glossary.label: simulation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The stated technical meaning; distinct disciplinary senses are identified where the site uses them.
public_glossary.short_definition: A simulation executes a model of a process to study the behaviour that follows from the model's rules and inputs.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A simulation executes a model of a process to study the behaviour that follows from the model's rules and inputs.
public_glossary.card_definition: Simulation permits controlled experiments when direct observation is costly, slow, dangerous, or impossible. Its results describe the modelled system and inherit the model's assumptions, simplifications, and parameter choices.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A simulation result is conditional on the model, initial conditions, parameters, numerical method, and random inputs; agreement within the simulation is distinct from validation against observations of the target system.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A simulation represents selected features of a process and calculates how that representation evolves. Deterministic simulations replay fixed equations or rules, while stochastic simulations sample uncertain events, often many times, to estimate a distribution of outcomes. Resolution, discretization, parameter choice, and random seeds can materially change the result. Verification asks whether the program implements the intended model; validation asks whether that model adequately represents the real system for the proposed use. A simulation can expose consequences, sensitivities, and failure modes without establishing that the same behaviour occurs outside the model.
public_glossary.scope_note: A simulation result is conditional on the model, initial conditions, parameters, numerical method, and random inputs; agreement within the simulation is distinct from validation against observations of the target system.

public_glossary.label: smooth function
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In number theory, a smooth integer has only small prime factors; that distinct meaning already belongs to smooth_number.
public_glossary.short_definition: A smooth function has continuous derivatives of every finite order in its stated mathematical setting.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A smooth function has continuous derivatives of every finite order in its stated mathematical setting.
public_glossary.card_definition: Every polynomial is smooth, including at points where its first derivative is zero. Smoothness allows repeated differentiation but does not imply that a real function equals its Taylor series. A function can therefore be smooth without being analytic.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read smooth as C-infinity unless the source explicitly gives a finite differentiability class such as C-one or C-two.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A smooth, or C-infinity, function has derivatives of every order and all those derivatives are continuous. For maps between Euclidean spaces, this means every iterated partial derivative exists and is continuous. On manifolds the definition is made through smooth coordinate charts. Smoothness is a regularity condition, not a claim of analyticity, convexity, or absence of critical points. In optimization prose, a smooth cell often means a region where the active formula and its derivatives vary smoothly; boundaries where the active branch changes may fail to share that regularity.
public_glossary.scope_note: Read smooth as C-infinity unless the source explicitly gives a finite differentiability class such as C-one or C-two.
public_glossary.example: Every polynomial map is smooth on its whole Euclidean domain.
public_glossary.non_example: The absolute-value function is not smooth at zero because it is not differentiable there.

public_glossary.label: smooth number
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A positive integer is y-smooth if none of its prime factors exceeds y.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A positive integer is y-smooth if none of its prime factors exceeds y.
public_glossary.card_definition: More generally, it is smooth over a specified set of primes if all its prime factors belong to that set. For example, 72 = 2³·3² is 3-smooth, while 70 has prime factors 2, 5, and 7.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The bound or allowed prime set is part of the definition.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The number 1 qualifies because it has no prime factors. The papers use smoothness to restrict which integers enter a sequence or reciprocal sum, often producing a structured but sparse collection.
public_glossary.scope_note: Integer smoothness relative to a named bound or a named set of primes.
public_glossary.example: 60 = 2² × 3 × 5 is {2,3,5}-smooth and is not 3-smooth, because 5 exceeds 3.
public_glossary.non_example: A smooth curve in the plane is a geometric notion, not this arithmetic one.

public_glossary.label: snapshot
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The stated technical meaning; distinct disciplinary senses are identified where the site uses them.
public_glossary.short_definition: A snapshot is a captured representation of data or system state associated with a particular point or version.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A snapshot is a captured representation of data or system state associated with a particular point or version.
public_glossary.card_definition: A database snapshot can preserve records as they appeared at noon; a repository snapshot can preserve one commit. Later changes do not make that snapshot inaccurate, but they do make it stale as a description of current state.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Snapshot meaning depends on capture time, scope, consistency guarantees, source version, included external state, and whether content is copied or referenced immutably.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Snapshots support comparison, recovery, audit, and reproducibility by fixing a view that would otherwise change. They may be full copies, incremental differences, filesystem references, database-consistent views, or application exports. Capturing related systems at different moments can create an internally inconsistent composite. A snapshot also may omit caches, secrets, running processes, external services, or uncommitted changes. Restoring it recreates only the state actually captured, and a successful restore does not establish that newer dependent systems remain compatible.
public_glossary.scope_note: Snapshot meaning depends on capture time, scope, consistency guarantees, source version, included external state, and whether content is copied or referenced immutably.

public_glossary.label: software library
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A software library is a reusable collection of code, interfaces, or formal definitions intended for other programs or developments to use.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A software library is a reusable collection of code, interfaces, or formal definitions intended for other programs or developments to use.
public_glossary.card_definition: Libraries can be source packages, compiled objects, runtime modules, or formal collections such as Mathlib. Their exposed interfaces supply reusable operations or results. Consumers depend on the relevant version, behaviour, licence, and compatibility with other parts of their program or proof development.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a result depends on a software library, record the exact package, version or revision, relevant interface assumptions, and environment used.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A library differs from an application because it primarily supplies capabilities to consumers rather than owning the whole interaction, although packages can contain both. Public interfaces form the supported contract; internal implementation may change between compatible releases. Static and dynamic libraries link differently, while interpreted packages load through a runtime. Formal libraries contribute checked definitions and theorems. Dependency updates can alter behavior or proof meaning, so reproducibility requires pinned identity and transitive dependencies, not merely the library’s familiar name.
public_glossary.scope_note: Qualified software and formal-library sense; the physical collection or lending institution is outside this row.
public_glossary.example: Mathlib is a formal software library supplying maintained Lean definitions and theorems.
public_glossary.non_example: A physical lending library uses another sense of the word; the qualified term here concerns reusable software or formal material.

public_glossary.label: source
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Source means the identified material that originates or controls the fact under discussion. A component may point to a committed code path, while a mathematical claim may point to a theorem, paper, or proof file and an execution claim may point to its run record. A nearby summary is not automatically authoritative source material.
public_glossary.short_definition: A source is the original or controlling material from which a particular claim or artifact is drawn.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A source is the original or controlling material from which a particular claim or artifact is drawn.

public_glossary.label: squarefree
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The absence of repeated prime factors for integers or repeated irreducible factors for nonzero polynomials; polynomial factorisation is relative to the stated coefficient field.
public_glossary.short_definition: Squarefree means having no repeated prime factor for an integer, or no repeated irreducible factor for a nonzero polynomial.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Squarefree means having no repeated prime factor for an integer, or no repeated irreducible factor for a nonzero polynomial.
public_glossary.card_definition: The integer 30=2·3·5 is squarefree, while 12=2²·3 is not. Over the complex numbers, a nonzero polynomial is squarefree exactly when every root is simple: (z−1)(z+1) qualifies, while (z−1)² does not.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The integer 1 and nonzero constant polynomials are squarefree; zero is not. Polynomial factors are taken over the specified coefficient field.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The same idea removes repeated factors in two settings. An irreducible polynomial factor cannot be split into lower-degree factors over its coefficient field. Over the complex numbers every nonconstant polynomial splits into linear factors, so squarefreeness becomes distinctness of roots, equivalently no common root of p and p′. The number-theory papers use squarefree integers in counting arguments, while the lemniscate papers use squarefree polynomials to control root geometry. These applications share a factorisation property without treating integers and polynomials as the same objects.
public_glossary.scope_note: Integer and polynomial uses both occur in the papers; the surrounding statement supplies the domain and coefficient field.
public_glossary.example: 30 is a squarefree integer, and z²−1 is a squarefree polynomial over the complex numbers.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: stack trace
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A diagnostic record of active or recent function calls leading to a program point or failure, distinct from repository revision history.
public_glossary.short_definition: A stack trace is a recorded list of active function calls at or near the point where a program failed or was inspected.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A stack trace is a recorded list of active function calls at or near the point where a program failed or was inspected.
public_glossary.card_definition: It usually names functions, files, and line numbers from the newest call back through its callers. It helps locate an execution path but may expose local paths or sensitive values.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use a stack trace to locate the failing path, then inspect the error, inputs, code, and environment before assigning cause.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A stack trace is diagnostic evidence about control flow, not a complete explanation of a failure. Optimisation, asynchronous execution, omitted frames, or generated code can make it incomplete or indirect. Plectis distinguishes reporting a degraded provider result from terminating with a stack trace. Public reports should redact private paths and secrets while retaining enough frames to diagnose the failure.
public_glossary.scope_note: Use a stack trace to locate the failing path, then inspect the error, inputs, code, and environment before assigning cause.
public_glossary.example: A Python traceback lists the failing line and the functions that called it.

public_glossary.label: stochastic
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Stochastic describes a process or model whose outcomes involve probability or randomness.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Stochastic describes a process or model whose outcomes involve probability or randomness.
public_glossary.card_definition: A stochastic procedure can follow precise rules while producing different outcomes across runs because it samples random choices. Analysis describes distributions, expectations, variability, or event probabilities rather than one guaranteed path. Pseudorandom software also depends on a generator and seed.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Separate randomness in the model from uncertainty about the model, and record seeds when exact computational repetition matters.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A stochastic process, model, or algorithm includes outcomes governed by probability. Its rules may be exact even though individual runs differ, so analysis concerns distributions, expected values, variability, dependence, or event probabilities rather than one fixed path. Computational randomness is normally pseudorandom and becomes repeatable when the generator, seed, implementation, and relevant ordering are fixed. Stochastic variation differs from ignorance about model choice or data quality. A reported sample illustrates possible behavior; it does not alone characterize the underlying probability law or justify a causal conclusion.
public_glossary.scope_note: Ordinary statistical usage.

public_glossary.label: subcover
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The stated technical sense; the related interfaces and mathematical objects are distinguished explicitly.
public_glossary.short_definition: A subcover is a selection from a collection of covering sets that still covers the same target set.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A subcover is a selection from a collection of covering sets that still covers the same target set.
public_glossary.card_definition: If three open intervals cover [0,1] and two of those intervals already cover every point of [0,1], those two form a subcover. A finite subcover uses finitely many members of the original collection; it need not be the smallest possible choice.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The selected sets must come from the given cover; replacing them with a newly invented covering set does not produce a subcover.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Compactness requires a finite subcover for every open cover. The condition is stronger than the existence of one finite open cover: any subset of the real line is covered by the whole real line, but many subsets are not compact. The empty collection covers the empty set, so it is a finite subcover when the target is empty. These distinctions keep the quantifiers in compactness arguments precise.

public_glossary.label: subexponential growth
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Asymptotic analysis. Subexponential does not mean slow or polynomial.
public_glossary.short_definition: Growth slower than every fixed exponential c^n with c>1.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Growth slower than every fixed exponential c^n with c>1.
public_glossary.card_definition: Polynomial growth n¹⁰ is subexponential because n¹⁰/cⁿ→0 for every fixed c>1. The faster function exp(√n) is also subexponential, showing that subexponential does not mean polynomial or practically small.
public_glossary.reader_rule: For positive sequences aₙ≥1, a standard equivalent condition is log(aₙ)/n→0. The comparison must hold against every fixed exponential base greater than one, rather than against just one especially large base.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In the reciprocal-tail analysis, normalized vanishing can constrain denominator states to subexponential growth. That scale restriction then limits how frequently strict divisibility changes can occur, but it does not make the states bounded or convergent.
public_glossary.scope_note: For positive sequences aₙ≥1, a standard equivalent condition is log(aₙ)/n→0. The comparison must hold against every fixed exponential base greater than one, rather than against just one especially large base.

public_glossary.label: subharmonic function
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Subharmonicity compares a value with nearby averages. It differs from convexity, which compares values along line segments.
public_glossary.short_definition: A subharmonic function never exceeds its average on a small surrounding circle and satisfies an upper-semicontinuity condition that rules out downward jumps at a point.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A subharmonic function never exceeds its average on a small surrounding circle and satisfies an upper-semicontinuity condition that rules out downward jumps at a point.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, |z|² is subharmonic: its average around a circle centred at z is larger than its value at z. A harmonic function has equality. Subharmonic functions may take the value −∞, as log|f| does at a zero of a holomorphic function f.
public_glossary.reader_rule: For twice differentiable real functions on a planar domain, subharmonicity is equivalent to a nonnegative Laplacian. The average condition is the more general definition and requires upper semicontinuity; it is not ordinary convexity along every line.
public_glossary.deep_definition: On a plane domain, the standard definition requires upper semicontinuity, local integrability, and the sub-mean inequality on discs contained in the domain; one usually excludes the function identically −∞. Upper semicontinuity means nearby limiting values cannot exceed the value at the point. The papers apply subharmonicity to squared moduli of analytic quantities, bounding an interior value by an average that can be evaluated using coefficients.
public_glossary.scope_note: For twice differentiable real functions on a planar domain, subharmonicity is equivalent to a nonnegative Laplacian. The average condition is the more general definition and requires upper semicontinuity; it is not ordinary convexity along every line.
public_glossary.example: The function |z|² is subharmonic because its circular average around a point exceeds its central value.

public_glossary.label: subsequence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Sequences and limits. Do not confuse subsequence with a consecutive block.
public_glossary.short_definition: A sequence formed by retaining terms at increasing indices.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A sequence formed by retaining terms at increasing indices.
public_glossary.card_definition: From 1,2,3,4,…, selecting indices 2,4,6,… produces the subsequence 2,4,6,…. Selecting square indices produces 1,4,9,16,…. Terms retain their original order although the gaps between chosen indices may grow.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A subsequence has form a_{n₁}, a_{n₂}, … with n₁ < n₂ < …. It need not be consecutive, but it preserves order. Every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Sparse exceptional behavior may survive along a subsequence even when its proportion among all indices tends to zero. Consequently, typical or density-one estimates may be insufficient when a proof must exclude infinitely recurring exceptional denominator states.

public_glossary.label: subsum
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A subsum is a sum obtained by retaining selected terms of a series and omitting the others.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A subsum is a sum obtained by retaining selected terms of a series and omitting the others.
public_glossary.card_definition: If A is the selected index set, the expression is ∑ over n in A of aₙ. The resulting sequence of retained terms forms a subseries, whose sum must be defined when the selection is infinite.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Convergence of the original series alone need not guarantee convergence of every subseries.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For absolutely convergent series, every subseries converges. For nonnegative convergent series, subsums lie between zero and the full sum; their possible values can form an interesting set.
public_glossary.scope_note: The selection is a set of indices, so a subsum is determined by which terms are included, not by any reordering.
public_glossary.example: One quarter plus one sixteenth is a subsum of the series of reciprocal powers of two.

public_glossary.short_definition: A sum is the result of adding quantities together.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A sum is the result of adding quantities together.
public_glossary.card_definition: A finite sum adds a specified number of terms. An infinite series uses the limit of finite partial sums when that limit exists. The symbol ∑ abbreviates a sum with its index and range stated alongside it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The range and order of summation can be part of the mathematical claim.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The papers distinguish exact finite arithmetic from conclusions about infinite sums. Passing from one to the other requires convergence and, when terms are rearranged, the appropriate justification for that rearrangement.

public_glossary.non_example: 3 × 4 is a product, not a sum.

public_glossary.reader_preview: The smallest number greater than or equal to every member of a set.

public_glossary.label: Taylor series
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The series determined by derivatives at a point; equality with the original function is an additional analytic property.
public_glossary.short_definition: A Taylor series is the power series whose coefficients are determined by a function’s derivatives at a chosen point.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A Taylor series is the power series whose coefficients are determined by a function’s derivatives at a chosen point.
public_glossary.card_definition: For one variable, the coefficient of (x−c)ⁿ is f⁽ⁿ⁾(c)/n!. The exponential has Taylor series 1+x+x²/2!+… at zero. Its partial sums give polynomial approximations, with error controlled by a separate remainder estimate.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Having derivatives of all orders does not ensure that the Taylor series converges or equals the function. Analyticity supplies local equality.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For example, exp(−1/x²), extended by zero at x = 0, is smooth and has every derivative zero there, yet it is positive elsewhere. Its Taylor series at zero therefore misses those values. Finite Taylor approximations and infinite series equality make different claims.
public_glossary.scope_note: Having derivatives of all orders does not ensure that the Taylor series converges or equals the function. Analyticity supplies local equality.

public_glossary.short_definition: Telemetry is automatically collected operational data sent or stored for observing a system away from the point where events occur.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Telemetry is automatically collected operational data sent or stored for observing a system away from the point where events occur.
public_glossary.card_definition: Request counts, error rates, timings, resource use, and selected event traces can be telemetry. It describes instrumented observations, not a complete or neutral record of everything the system did.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Telemetry is defined by its events, sampling, fields, aggregation, retention, transmission, access controls, and relationship to the system state being inferred.

A dashboard is a presentation of telemetry rather than the raw evidence itself. Interpreting a change requires checking definitions and collection changes before concluding that the underlying system or user behavior changed.

public_glossary.label: threshold

public_glossary.short_definition: A threshold is a boundary value at which a classification, condition, or behavior changes.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A threshold is a boundary value at which a classification, condition, or behavior changes.
public_glossary.card_definition: A temperature may cross a physical threshold, a theorem may apply when x exceeds 10, or a score may trigger an alert above 0.8. The boundary can arise from nature, mathematics, convention, or policy.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A threshold includes a measured quantity, comparison direction, boundary value, and consequence; equality at the boundary must be specified when it matters.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Some thresholds are discovered properties, such as the value where a mathematical regime changes. A threshold need not be selected by policy, and a policy threshold need not reveal a natural discontinuity in the underlying phenomenon. Units, calibration, population, and uncertainty affect interpretation. Crossing a noisy threshold once may not indicate a stable change, while hysteresis or repeated evidence can prevent rapid switching near the boundary.

public_glossary.label: timeout
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The stated technical meaning; distinct disciplinary senses are identified where the site uses them.
public_glossary.short_definition: A timeout ends or changes waiting behavior when a defined time limit expires before the awaited event is observed.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A timeout ends or changes waiting behavior when a defined time limit expires before the awaited event is observed.
public_glossary.card_definition: A client may stop waiting after 30 seconds so one slow call cannot block forever. The server or background job may nevertheless continue and later produce a result.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Timeout semantics specify which clock starts, the duration, the event being awaited, whether underlying work is cancelled, and how late completion or repeated attempts are handled.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Connection, read, idle, operation, and overall timeouts measure different intervals. Expiry means the waiting side did not observe completion in time; it does not prove that remote work failed, stopped, or had no side effects. Retrying after a timeout can therefore duplicate effects. Short limits improve responsiveness but may reject legitimate slow work, while long limits consume resources and delay recovery. Cancellation support, idempotency, status lookup, and late-result reconciliation determine whether timeout handling remains correct under uncertainty.

public_glossary.label: TLS
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The protocol that protects network communication with encryption, integrity checks, and peer authentication; encoding data is not equivalent protection.
public_glossary.short_definition: Transport Layer Security, or TLS, is a protocol that encrypts and authenticates a network connection.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Transport Layer Security, or TLS, is a protocol that encrypts and authenticates a network connection.
public_glossary.card_definition: HTTPS uses TLS to protect HTTP traffic while it travels between client and server. Certificates help the client verify the server identity associated with a hostname.
public_glossary.reader_rule: TLS protects transport between endpoints; it does not make endpoint software, stored data, or response content trustworthy.
public_glossary.deep_definition: During a TLS handshake, peers agree on cryptographic parameters, establish session keys, and usually authenticate the server with a certificate chain. The resulting channel protects confidentiality and integrity against ordinary network interception. Certificate checks, supported protocol versions, and key management affect the guarantee. Plectis HTTPS links depend on this transport layer, while content evidence and publication authority remain separate questions.
public_glossary.scope_note: TLS protects transport between endpoints; it does not make endpoint software, stored data, or response content trustworthy.

public_glossary.label: total variation distance
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Probability and statistics. Different from total variation of a real function or path.
public_glossary.short_definition: Total variation distance is the supremum of the absolute difference between the probabilities two distributions assign to the same event.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Total variation distance is the supremum of the absolute difference between the probabilities two distributions assign to the same event.
public_glossary.card_definition: For finite outcomes, total variation distance is half the sum of the absolute differences between two probability tables. It ranges from 0 for identical distributions to 1 when the distributions concentrate on disjoint events.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Equivalently, take the largest difference in probability assigned to the same measurable event. Any test valued between 0 and 1 changes in expectation by at most this distance, but arithmetic properties of particular outcomes need not be preserved.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The prime-gap countermodel keeps short-block empirical laws close in total variation while altering the target denominator behavior. This demonstrates that strong statistical resemblance can coexist with decisive arithmetic difference. Total variation here compares probability measures, not the variation of a curve or function.
public_glossary.scope_note: Equivalently, take the largest difference in probability assigned to the same measurable event. Any test valued between 0 and 1 changes in expectation by at most this distance, but arithmetic properties of particular outcomes need not be preserved.

public_glossary.label: totient
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Euler's totient φ(n) counts the integers from 1 through n that are coprime to the positive integer n.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Euler's totient φ(n) counts the integers from 1 through n that are coprime to the positive integer n.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, φ(6) = 2 because only 1 and 5 are coprime to 6 in that range. The definition gives φ(1) = 1; for n greater than 1, the qualifying integers are all strictly smaller than n.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The input must be a positive integer in this definition.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The papers use the totient in arithmetic series. Its values encode how prime factors restrict coprimality, linking multiplicative structure with questions about sums and digit expansions.
public_glossary.scope_note: A totient result covers the function as defined, not related functions.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #249 asks whether the sum of the totient of n over two to the n is irrational.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: transaction
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A transaction groups related operations behind a stated validation and commitment boundary, with guarantees that depend on the system.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A transaction groups related operations behind a stated validation and commitment boundary, with guarantees that depend on the system.
public_glossary.card_definition: A database transaction may promise ACID properties at a documented isolation level. A user or workflow transaction may instead stage actions, validate them, obtain authorization, and commit or abandon selected changes. Those looser uses must not silently inherit strict database guarantees.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Readers should ask which actions participate, when commitment occurs, what concurrent observers can see, and which effects rollback can actually reverse.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Transaction is a family of consistency patterns rather than a universal promise of database ACID behavior. A database transaction may provide atomicity, consistency constraints, isolation, and durability at a stated level. A user or workflow transaction may instead stage changes, validate them, request authorization, then commit or abandon the operation, with weaker recovery guarantees. External messages, network calls, files, and irreversible effects may sit outside the boundary. Readers should ask which actions participate, what validation precedes commitment, how concurrent activity is handled, and what rollback can truly restore.
public_glossary.scope_note: Covers database and workflow commitment boundaries. Only a transaction that explicitly promises atomicity may be described as all-or-none.
public_glossary.example: A workflow stages candidate changes, validates them, obtains authorization, and then commits selected effects while recording any external actions outside rollback.
public_glossary.non_example: Calling a multi-file operation transactional does not guarantee that remote messages, deployments, or partially written files can all be reversed.

public_glossary.label: transcendental
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A number is transcendental if it is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A number is transcendental if it is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients.
public_glossary.card_definition: Equivalently, it is not algebraic over the rational numbers. Familiar examples include π and e. Every real transcendental number is irrational, but some irrational numbers, such as √2, are algebraic.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The polynomial must be nonzero: the zero polynomial vanishes at every number.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Proving irrationality alone therefore does not establish transcendence. A transcendence argument must rule out every nonzero integer-coefficient polynomial relation, which is a stronger requirement than ruling out fractions.
public_glossary.scope_note: Transcendence of one series says nothing about a related series until a proof connects them.
public_glossary.example: Pi and e are transcendental; the square root of two is not.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: triangle inequality
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Metrics, norms, and absolute values. Equality requires special alignment conditions.
public_glossary.short_definition: The distance directly between two points is at most the length of any route through a third.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The distance directly between two points is at most the length of any route through a third.
public_glossary.card_definition: For numbers, |x+y|≤|x|+|y|. Geometrically, traveling from A to C through B cannot be shorter than the direct distance from A to C. Equality needs the two steps to align without backtracking.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The triangle inequality combines upper bounds after decomposing a quantity. Its reverse form, ||x|-|y||≤|x-y|, gives a lower bound on separation from differing sizes. Both depend on the relevant absolute value, norm, or metric.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Path and polynomial estimates assemble local pieces using triangle inequalities. The step can lose crucial cancellation, so a proof needing a sharp constant may require additional angle, sign, orthogonality, or convexity information rather than repeated triangle bounds.
public_glossary.scope_note: The triangle inequality combines upper bounds after decomposing a quantity. Its reverse form, ||x|-|y||≤|x-y|, gives a lower bound on separation from differing sizes. Both depend on the relevant absolute value, norm, or metric.

public_glossary.label: trinomial
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Terms are counted after equal powers have been combined and zero coefficients removed.
public_glossary.short_definition: A trinomial is a polynomial written as the sum of three nonzero terms.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A trinomial is a polynomial written as the sum of three nonzero terms.
public_glossary.card_definition: For example, z⁵+2z²−7 is a trinomial. The exponents need not be consecutive, and a missing power simply has coefficient zero. The paper studies the form zⁿ+azᵐ+b.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Count nonzero terms after combining like powers. A nominal three-term expression can simplify to a binomial if coefficients cancel. “Monic trinomial” additionally says the coefficient of the highest-degree term is one.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Trinomial describes presentation by three terms, not irreducibility, degree three, or possession of three roots. A cubic is classified by degree; a trinomial is classified by how many nonzero monomials appear.
public_glossary.scope_note: Count nonzero terms after combining like powers. A nominal three-term expression can simplify to a binomial if coefficients cancel. “Monic trinomial” additionally says the coefficient of the highest-degree term is one.

public_glossary.label: truth maintenance
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Truth maintenance records each claim’s evidence, dependencies, invalidators, and action consequences; it does not guarantee truth or replace the source that owns the claim.
public_glossary.short_definition: Truth maintenance tracks claims together with their reasons and dependencies so they can be reconsidered when evidence changes.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Truth maintenance tracks claims together with their reasons and dependencies so they can be reconsidered when evidence changes.
public_glossary.card_definition: In AI and knowledge systems, this concerns managing beliefs and justifications. Plectis applies the idea to source records, checks, uncertainty, and decisions that depend on particular claims.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Tracking a belief is not a guarantee that the belief is true.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The useful behaviour is responding to a failed assumption or contradictory observation: identify affected conclusions, change their status, and review actions that relied on them rather than preserving an unsupported conclusion unchanged.
public_glossary.scope_note: Truth maintenance covers how beliefs, evidence, and their dependencies are tracked across the system's control plane, separating receipts, model outputs, generated projections, and doctrine commitments so none borrows another's authority. A reader meets it wherever a claim is shown with its supporting evidence, its status, or the conditions under which it would be withdrawn.

public_glossary.label: uniform convergence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Functions converge uniformly when one sufficiently late stage makes the error small simultaneously at every point of the stated domain.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Functions converge uniformly when one sufficiently late stage makes the error small simultaneously at every point of the stated domain.
public_glossary.card_definition: For every positive tolerance ε, there must be an N such that |fₙ(x) − f(x)| < ε for all n ≥ N and all x in the domain. The same N works for every x.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Pointwise convergence instead allows the threshold N to depend on x.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Uniform convergence preserves continuity of continuous functions in the usual metric setting. Passing strict inequalities or derivative bounds to a limit needs additional care; uniform convergence alone does not preserve every property.
public_glossary.scope_note: Pointwise convergence instead allows the threshold N to depend on x.

public_glossary.label: uninterpretable
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Here, uninterpretable describes work for which readers do not yet have an adequate account of what it says or why it works.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Here, uninterpretable describes work for which readers do not yet have an adequate account of what it says or why it works.
public_glossary.card_definition: A formal proof can check while its main idea, relationship to prior work, or intended meaning remains poorly explained. The missing task is to make that content understandable at an appropriate level of expertise.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The term describes a current gap in understanding, not a proof that understanding is impossible.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Useful exposition states the exact result, exposes the decisive argument, and preserves attribution and limits. Community understanding and use require further engagement beyond a machine's acceptance.
public_glossary.scope_note: Names a result that cannot yet be explained by a person. Related cards: digestion, exposition, formal verification.
public_glossary.example: A long kernel-accepted proof whose authors cannot say where the hard step was is uninterpretable in this sense.
public_glossary.non_example: An informal argument that a reader can repair and restate is interpretable even before it is formalised.

public_glossary.label: unit disc
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The open unit disc is the set of complex numbers z with |z| < 1.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The open unit disc is the set of complex numbers z with |z| < 1.
public_glossary.card_definition: It consists of points at distance less than one from the origin in the complex plane. The closed unit disc uses |z| ≤ 1 and includes its boundary, the unit circle |z| = 1.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Open and closed versions differ precisely at that boundary.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The lemniscate papers use conditions such as |p(z)| < 1. That says the polynomial's value lies in the open unit disc; it does not necessarily say the input point z lies there.
public_glossary.scope_note: Open unit disc in the complex plane unless a page specifies the closed disc.
public_glossary.example: 0 and 1/2 are in the open unit disc; 1 and i are on the unit circle, so not inside it.
public_glossary.non_example: A disc of radius 1 centred somewhere other than 0 is a different set.

public_glossary.label: univalent function
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Univalence means one-to-one on the whole specified domain, not merely near each point.
public_glossary.short_definition: A univalent function is a holomorphic function that is one-to-one on its domain.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A univalent function is a holomorphic function that is one-to-one on its domain.
public_glossary.card_definition: The function z↦z² is not univalent on the whole complex plane because z and -z have the same image, but it is univalent on a suitably chosen half-plane. A univalent map has no self-overlap on its stated domain.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Univalence is domain-relative and stronger than having nonzero derivative at one point. A holomorphic function with nonzero derivative is locally one-to-one, yet may still take the same value at distant points.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The paper needs the continued inverse branch to remain injective throughout a disc. That permits distortion and area estimates for its image; a many-to-one analytic map would count overlaps and invalidate that geometric reading.
public_glossary.scope_note: Univalence is domain-relative and stronger than having nonzero derivative at one point. A holomorphic function with nonzero derivative is locally one-to-one, yet may still take the same value at distant points.
public_glossary.example: The function z↦z² is not univalent on the whole complex plane because z and -z have the same image, but it is univalent on a suitably chosen half-plane.

public_glossary.label: universal quantifier
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The mathematical sense stated here; related software or ordinary-language uses are distinguished where relevant.
public_glossary.short_definition: A universal quantifier states that a property holds for every element of a specified domain.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A universal quantifier states that a property holds for every element of a specified domain.
public_glossary.card_definition: The symbol ∀ means “for every.” For example, ∀n ∈ ℕ, n+1 > n says that adding one increases every natural number. One counterexample would refute the statement; a finite sample usually cannot prove it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: The domain and the order of quantifiers determine the claim, including whether later choices can depend on earlier inputs.
public_glossary.deep_definition: “For every n, there exists m greater than n” permits a different m for each n. “There exists m greater than every n” asks for one choice working for all n. These statements have different truth values over the natural numbers.
public_glossary.scope_note: The domain and the order of quantifiers determine the claim, including whether later choices can depend on earlier inputs.

public_glossary.label: unramified prime
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Unramified means no multiplicity in the prime factorization upstairs. A prime can be unramified and still split into several primes.
public_glossary.short_definition: A prime is unramified in a number-field extension when its factorization upstairs contains no repeated prime-ideal power, equivalently every ramification index is one.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A prime is unramified in a number-field extension when its factorization upstairs contains no repeated prime-ideal power, equivalently every ramification index is one.
public_glossary.card_definition: In Q(i)/Q, odd rational primes are unramified. The prime 2 ramifies because the ideal (2) is the square of the prime ideal generated by 1+i. Only finitely many rational primes ramify in a fixed number field.
public_glossary.reader_rule: For a base prime p, “unramified in L” means that every prime ideal P above p has ramification index e(P/p)=1. This does not mean there is only one P above p. In the number-field setting the residue extensions are finite-field extensions and hence separable.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In a number-field extension, the ideal generated by p factors as a product ∏P_i^{e_i}. Ramification occurs when some exponent e_i exceeds one. The cited argument selects rational primes for which every exponent is one before prescribing Frobenius behavior. This provides the controlled residue-field symmetry used later.
public_glossary.scope_note: For a base prime p, “unramified in L” means that every prime ideal P above p has ramification index e(P/p)=1. This does not mean there is only one P above p. In the number-field setting the residue extensions are finite-field extensions and hence separable.
public_glossary.example: In Q(i)/Q, odd primes are unramified, while 2 ramifies because (2) is the square of the Gaussian prime ideal generated by 1+i, up to a unit.

public_glossary.label: upstream
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The stated technical meaning; distinct disciplinary senses are identified where the site uses them.
public_glossary.short_definition: Upstream describes a source or earlier stage whose output, changes, or decisions flow into a specified consumer.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Upstream describes a source or earlier stage whose output, changes, or decisions flow into a specified consumer.
public_glossary.card_definition: An upstream repository can supply imported code, an upstream service can answer requests, and an upstream pipeline stage can produce input for later stages. The direction is always relative to a named flow.
public_glossary.reader_rule: An object is upstream only with respect to a particular dependency or data path, and the same object may be downstream in another relationship.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Upstream names direction in a flow of code, data, work, or authority. A fork receives changes from its upstream repository; a processing stage receives records from an earlier producer; a service may depend on an upstream service for responses. Changes or failures can propagate to downstream consumers even when their local files or configuration remain untouched. The word does not identify ownership or superiority, and it has no absolute direction outside a stated relationship. In physical geography it retains its river meaning, while technical prose usually supplies repository, service, dependency, or pipeline context.

public_glossary.label: URL
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: URLs can address network resources, local files, or inline data. Keeping the same URL does not guarantee unchanged content.
public_glossary.short_definition: A URL is a structured identifier for a resource, commonly giving a network address and a way to access it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A URL is a structured identifier for a resource, commonly giving a network address and a way to access it.
public_glossary.card_definition: A web URL can contain a scheme such as `https`, a host, a path, a query, and a fragment. Not every URL names a remote file: a `data:` URL carries content directly, and a relative URL gets part of its meaning from a base URL.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a stable URL as a route to a resource, not proof that its current content is unchanged or trustworthy.
public_glossary.deep_definition: An absolute URL includes a scheme; a relative reference is resolved against a base, usually the current page. Queries can select a response, while fragments identify a part or view of the resource and are not included in an HTTP request. Plectis uses stable URLs and fragments so a link can return to the same guide, theorem, or glossary entry after the source files are reorganized.
public_glossary.scope_note: Treat a stable URL as a route to a resource, not proof that its current content is unchanged or trustworthy.
public_glossary.example: `https://example.org/docs/guide.html#setup` locates the setup section of a web document.
public_glossary.non_example: A filesystem path without a URL scheme or web base is not automatically a public URL.
